#2794. Fantasy Football: Offenses that surged — and slumped — in NFL season's second month

Few things in life excite me more than offensive ecosystem talk. Deployment of players, weaponizing concepts and schemes; it's the best.

Figuring out the right offensive environments can also be our best path to uncovering value and ascending players in fantasy football. With eight weeks of data, we can see which teams have improved since the start of the season and which are going in the other direction. I'll spend more time on the improving teams and quickly explain why the fallers rank where they do right now. We'll use a metric I came up with to do it.

My Offensive Efficiency Score is simply the average of each team's rank across metrics I use to measure a unit's effectiveness (dropback EPA, rush EPA, points per drive, drive scoring rate, success rate and explosive play rate). Nothing special. However, the variety of variables accounts for teams that attack in different ways — teams that move the ball successfully but aren't explosive get measured the same as an inverse team.

Here's how the league stacks up after eight weeks.

Offensive efficiency scores for all 32 NFL teams through Week 8.

Quietly, plenty of interesting things are happening in the Dolphins offense. In a league full of humiliating units, this isn't one of them. Miami looks put together, well-coached and runs plenty of sound concepts.

While not flush with household names, young skill-position talents like boundary rookie receiver Caleb Douglas, slot-man Malik Washington and especially Ollie Gordon at running back have offered strong moments. The run game has taken off with Gordon at the helm, as the team has leaned into gap concepts. They rank sixth in yards per carry on gap runs and only the Patriots and Titans run it at a higher rate.

Miami has a stretch of games against the Lions, Colts, Bills and Jets defenses coming over the next month. You can play some of these Dolphins options against those weaker stop units.

After three brutal games to start the year against some of the best defenses in the league, the Patriots offense has been on fire over the past month.

That schedule caveat might be necessary but it's also fair to point out that Drake Maye has been getting it done without a stacked hand. A.J. Brown has been injured and not impactful when he's played, while other role players have stepped up. The offensive line has dealt with injuries and the run game remains middling.

Maye is back in the elite quarterback territory with his play over this recent stretch. Week 9's matchup against the Packers will be telling, especially as we assess how many of these young pass-catchers he can take with him to fantasy relevance.

The Steelers finished 31st and 30th in Weeks 1 and 2 in the offensive efficiency metric. They have ranked between fourth and 18th in every week since, with three finishes in the top eight.

The Steelers have really leaned into a bully ball mentality. From Week 5 on they use jumbo personnel (six offensive linemen) on 11.5% of their plays, the third-highest rate in the league. They slowed down their pace, pass rates and have gotten under center more often. This has led to the explosion of Jaylen Warren, who has flat-out been one of the best running backs in the NFL. Pittsburgh ranks first in rushing EPA in this span.

The passing game under Aaron Rodgers isn't quite as effective (23rd) but they do find some steady plays in the quick game and weaponize their tight ends. I enjoy watching this offense much more now than I did early in the season and it's no longer a "hands-off" environment for fantasy.

Washington has ranked between 10th and 15th in all three of their games in this span. Based on the current personnel, it's tough to imagine this team featuring a high ceiling but the floor is strong, as long as Jayden Daniels stays healthy.

That means we can at least consider the highly involved players as flex candidates in the right matchup. Antonio Williams ran the most routes on the team last week and is on track for a strong post-bye rookie bump.

The Jets attack is one of the most improved offensive units in the NFL this season, up from 31st in 2025 to 11th overall this year. They've gotten even better the last month with Braelon Allen breaking out and Omar Cooper Jr. excelling as a rookie.

The challenge for fantasy is this unit's crowded nature. They got three-deep at receiver with Cooper, Garrett Wilson and AD Mitchell, have two highly drafted tight ends and two strong backs when Breece Hall returns. You felt the consequences when Cooper failed to record a target last week, despite good film, and Mitchell went off against the Raiders.

With the unit looking viable and the defense struggling, we should get some good scripts for the Jets offense to put up points. We'll just have to try and pinpoint the right matchups.

The Texans have four top-seven weekly finishes in the efficiency metric this season. There have been some real frustrations with this unit and I have a decently long list of complaints but C.J. Stroud is playing well enough to cover up some of the sins.

The Texans need to give up on being this run-heavy unit and really lean into the passing game given Stroud's play and the receiver depth. The Texans ranked fifth, 10th and eighth in pass rate over expected from Weeks 4 to 6 but dipped down to 21st in Week 7 before their bye. How they approach this week's game coming back from their bye week will tell us a lot about whether OC Nick Caley is up for changing his stripes.

On the season, Green Bay ranks 11th in dropback EPA and 31st in rushing. That 20-point gap is tied for the second-largest in the NFL. I don't have much faith the Packers will improve on the ground. The current version of Josh Jacobs isn't enough to fix the struggling unit, despite his fantasy production, and the offensive line is the load-bearing issue.

As such, I expect this team to continue to be pass-centric and as long as they lean into that, they should be able to improve in these rankings over the course of the season.

The Bucs have gone the other way of some of the last couple of teams discussed and fully leaned into their rushing attack. Over the last two weeks, Baker Mayfield has completed seven of his 14 pass attempts. The Bucs won both games.

The Bucs have leaned into more gap runs as the season has gone on and the offensive line is responding with some excellent play. Over the last four weeks, they rank third in explosive rushing rate. Bucky Irving was one of the best running back selections this year.

Cam Ward is coming off the best game of his NFL career. That is buoying the jump in the rankings, as they were the sixth-best offense in Week 8 but no better than 19th in any other.

The Titans leaned into no huddle on 41% of their plays in Week 8, their highest rate of the season by far. This could be an aberration against the Bengals defense but I'm open to the possibility that a spread offense with a high pass rate (fifth in pass rate over expected) just suits Ward better.

The Ravens were pacing to be an elite offense early in the season. Everything has fallen apart with Lamar Jackson's injury. He looks likely to miss the rest of the season, as does his backup Tyler Huntley.

The Ravens traded for Jacoby Brissett on Wednesday, the best outcome they could hope for given the miserable situation they're in. Brissett has familiarity with the coaching staff and should pick up the offense in time to start in Week 10. He's enough to keep the ship afloat and keep Baltimore out of the league basement by the end of the season.

The Saints desperately need to get left tackle Kelvin Banks back. You can directly map their offensive collapse with his removal from the offense. Banks is back at practice this week, so his return in the next few games will go a long way toward saving this unit.

Hopefully, he can also elevate what's been one of the NFL's least effective run games. The team also desperately needs Travis Etienne Jr. to come back and be the player they paid him to be this offseason. The current stable of backs just won't cut it.

Injuries along the offensive line have sunk a unit that was one of the most enjoyable in September. They've ranked 23rd and 24th the last two weeks. Unfortunately, if they can't get an infusion of health along that line, they don't stand a chance at matching their September numbers against quality opponents.

The Falcons are unfairly penalized by a monsoon game in Tampa Bay in Week 8, where Michael Penix Jr. completely collapsed. Otherwise, they've hovered between 14th and 20th in Weeks 5 to 7. I think that's probably more appropriate for their current standing — an average NFL offense that can spike due to high-end talent in Drake London and Bijan Robinson.

Two games against the Seahawks and Broncos have set back the once-soaring Chiefs. It's also shown that if you can shut down their explosive ground game, they don't have the horses to throw on good defenses. The Chiefs need to get serious about their receiver issues for once and make a trade before the deadline. It's that simple.

You can totally ignore this one. The Bears are unfairly penalized by a 28th-place ranking in Week 5, Tyson Bagent's disaster and final start against the Packers. They've ranked 13th, seventh and fifth in Caleb Williams' three games since returning from injury. Chicago is one of the best offenses in the NFL; I have no doubt.

It feels like everyone wants to find one smoking gun that's behind the Seahawks stalling on offense but it's not that simple — despite the inclination to crush OC Brian Fleury for being unable to mimic Klint Kubiak's 2025 output. There's blame to go around.

The offensive line has been spotty but you hope that improves with Quenton Nelson settling in at left guard. The run game needs Jadarian Price to break out as a more explosive option. Sam Darnold also hasn't played well and now he's set to miss some time with an injury. Drew Lock actually captained this team's second-best offensive outing in Week 2 this year. Lastly, while Jaxon Smith-Njigba can handle an immense share of the passing volume, the lack of a true second threat has held this unit back. The extra attention he's received this year has also forced Darnold to make too many post-snap decisions, which is the biggest reason he's struggled.

Odds are, Seattle can fix one or two problems on that long list. It's not ideal that the ledger goes as deep as it does. Even if they fix a couple, I still think this tops out as an average unit overall.

The Colts' season is over. They know it; they've acted on it. I don't think 26th is their floor. If/when Jonathan Taylor and even Josh Downs are shipped off this roster over the next week, you can make a strong argument that this is the least talented offense in the NFL. I won't be looking for much fantasy viability out of anyone on this team going forward.

#2792. Santoli: AI bull market almost surely needs tech stocks to recover to keep advancing

The road to bull-market glory does not run through Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway and Eli Lilly.

There's been a virtual buying panic in traditionally defensive, high-quality stocks over the past few weeks, a near-equal-and-opposite offset to the selling pressure in semiconductors and AI-build-out spenders. The three stocks above — the only members of the $1 trillion market-cap club not in Big Tech – have collectively added $550 billion in market value in the past month, almost making up for what Alphabet has lost.

The Nasdaq-100 and the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) are rushing toward one another in a satisfying picture of symmetry that nonetheless reflects an almost comical level of tactical rotation executed by an investment community accustomed to playing one factor against another.

While this to-and-fro has so far protected the S&P 500 as a whole from an appreciable setback for months, it has left it stymied around levels that date back to May — before we got two earnings-reporting seasons showing 30% annual profit growth.

A week ago here, I suggested the AI theme was nearing a make-or-break moment to stage a recovery or risk surrendering its leadership status and destabilizing the broader market. Thus far, this trade has failed to respond to moderate oversold conditions or a run of cosmetically strong hyperscaler quarterly results, further loosening its grip on the benefit of the doubt.

In stressed markets undergoing soul-searching about the long-term bullish thesis, prices often need to travel further to find buyers with conviction while the market action must disappoint dip-buyers to extinguish complacency. Hard to know if we're there, but presumably we're now closer.

The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday right at its 200-day moving average, off almost 11% from its record high. After an enervating failed Monday-morning bounce attempt, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index finished down another 3.8% and settled under the late-July low that was set as the Situational Awareness hedge fund was finished liquidating.

"Markets did not get the memo that bearish seasonal pressure typically subsides in mid-October and instead ended the month with some of the most acute selling pressure that has been realized during the late-summer/early-fall period," notes JPMorgan technical strategist Jason Hunter. He's advising clients to remain on the defensive "until we see clear evidence of a bottoming process on the charts or until there are clear signs of capitulation."

This is a time-tested playbook, though many a sharp market pullback has ended without what would qualify as unqualified capitulation.

The market action is winning some plaudits for the way non-tech stocks have held up better, many groups benefiting from the "quality" rotation while abandoned consumer cyclicals get a reprieve from easing oil prices and the slide in the 10-year Treasury yield back below 5%.

This gives active managers plenty to do in playing against a highly concentrated and tech-dependent S&P 500. But I'll continue to argue that the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market.

The AI-related stocks' weighting in the S&P 500 is off the highs but remains near 45%, according to Morgan Stanley.

As the chart shows, AI has wobbled relative to the rest of the market during this uptrend before reasserting itself.  But there's a trickier element to the current gut check: In prior phases of the buildout, the key limiting bottleneck gave investors something to buy in order to exploit it.

The initial scarcity of GPUs meant to own Nvidia above all else from 2023 through 2024. When cloud capacity, power and cooling were found to be the crucial scarce resources, hyperscaler stocks worked and the AI-adjacent industrials were drastically revalued. Then memory emerged as the chokepoint and Micron and Sandisk went stratospheric.

Now, as Nvidia's Jensen Huang has said, capital is the constraint and that not only leaves no asset to buy, but it raises the cost of capital broadly as the mega-caps go free-cash-flow-negative.

Overlapping feedback loops and scrambled correlations across the markets and the real economy have further sapped investor conviction. Treasury yields no longer move with oil but largely with AI-capex sentiment, with both in retreat lately. AI-stock setbacks also mute inflation momentum and the equity wealth effect, meaning fewer Federal Reserve rate hikes are anticipated now versus a month ago.

This all probably sounds like an elaborate trap, and it has become one for the previously crowded trades. Could this reflect the end game for the AI-exuberance market chapter, which as I keep pointing out peaked around the SpaceX IPO in June? Impossible to say for sure, but if it were, I'm not sure things would look much different to this point.

But I don't want to dismiss the possibility that a lot of the known challenges are largely reflected in prices.

I argued in August that we should assume the valuation peak for this cycle was in. We've now retrenched to a forward P/E of 18.5 on the S&P 500 from 23 a year ago and the Nasdaq-100 at 20x is at the slimmest premium to the S&P 500 valuation in nine years. I'm on board with the idea that the market is telling us companies are now "over-earning," but if nothing else there is less valuation risk now than in recent months.

Sentiment toward AI stocks is in the dumps. Funds' positioning in tech has retreated below neutral. Important trading lows this year have happened near the turn of the month on March 30 and July 29, and the Nasdaq-100's relative-strength reading is exactly as oversold as it was at those turns.

So, stay alert for possible relief bounces that could evolve into something more consequential if indeed the midterm elections pass in a way that allows traders to unclench a bit into the year's home stretch.

John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "Similar to valuation, sentiment is not a timing tool, but it is getting harder and harder to find any bulls, as a near-perfect storm of tight financial conditions is being met with tech earnings that have gone from bad to worse in the blink of an eye."

-Another good big-picture conversation on the practical business and investment implications of the next phase of AI proliferation on Patrick O'Shaughnessy's Invest Like the Best podcast, this one with investor Cliff Sosin. His comparison of AI infrastructure economics to internet connectivity providers and his argument for how most of the productivity boost will go toward "consumer surplus" rather than corporate profits are particularly interesting.

-For my birthday Monday, my colleague and friend Sara Eisen wondered how I would write a birthday message to myself. I immediately regretted suggesting she ask ChatGPT, which generated this credible and somewhat embarrassing result:

"Another year older, though the longer-term trend remains constructive. Some modest deterioration in the underlying internals, perhaps, but nothing that suggests a decisive breakdown.

"The candles on the cake are approaching historically elevated levels, though valuation concerns have persisted for years without derailing the advance. At this stage, the key question isn't whether I've gotten older — that's largely priced in — but whether the wisdom gains can continue to offset the inevitable compression in energy multiples.

"For now, I'm maintaining a cautiously optimistic outlook, with upside optionality, downside support from family and friends, and no immediate need for Fed intervention. Happy birthday to me. The secular bull market remains intact."

The stampede into perceived defensive stocks has been a crucial driver of Apple shares' massive outperformance over the Nasdaq-100 since the AI-capex agita flared up months ago. Apple heading into Monday's earnings report had outperformed the Nasdaq-100 by nearly 20 percentage points over the prior six months.

Its singular refusal to join the aggressive spending binge to build AI capacity preserved its free cash flow and made it the perfect counterweight to the capex trade, while inflating Apple's valuation to a 15-year high.

But its advantage in free-cash-flow yield has now narrowed, thanks to its stock-price gains and the collapse of peer shares.

#2791. 'We were completely dominated' - Lens boss Yannick Cahuzac tells players to take 'a long, hard look' at themselves after historic 9-1 Champions League defeat to Como

Lens head coach Yannick Cahuzac has challenged his shell-shocked squad to confront some harsh truths after suffering a historic 9-1 Champions League thrashing at home to Como on Wednesday night. Cesc Fabregas' ruthless Italian visitors ran riot at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis to record the largest away victory in the tournament's history.

Cahuzac has ordered his players to take full responsibility after Lens were torn apart on their own turf by Serie A side Como on Matchday 4. Tasos Douvikas struck a treble and set up Nico Paz as the visitors matched the competition's joint-largest winning margin of eight goals alongside Liverpool in 2007 and Real Madrid in 2015. Lucas Da Cunha, Marc Oliver Kempf, Mattia Liberali, Martin Baturina and 18-year-old debutant Matteo Papaccioli also netted after an early penalty against Maxence Caqueret was overturned by VAR.

Speaking to UEFA's official website after the match, Cahuzac said: "It's a heavy scoreline, we were completely dominated. We've got to have a long, hard look at ourselves and attempt to regain some pride against Marseille on Sunday."

Demanding accountability from his players, he added: "We have to be able to each other in the eyes, tell each other the truth. We have to pick ourselves up and turn our attention to Sunday. Unfortunately, these things happen across the course of a career."

Reflecting on the collapse and Friday's 1-0 loss to Lille, he continued: "I can't offer you an in-depth analysis of what went wrong. We're hurting, but I'm going to concentrate on my side, and how we can pick them up from this.

"Each game is different. We've also had some good performances; we won three games on the bounce in the league prior to Friday [when they were beaten 1-0 by Lille]. Tonight, we can't talk about anything positive about our performance."

After volleying past Jean Butez in the 65th minute for the French club's only consolation goal of the evening, right-back Ruben Aguilar also spoke to UEFA's official website about their defensive breakdown: "We had a game plan, but we weren't able to execute it. We were cut through and everything went so quickly. We'll get back to work quickly. We're all shocked, saddened, downbeat. That's part of life as a footballer at the top level."

Vowing to make amends in front of their home supporters this weekend, Aguilar added: "Nine goals at home, we have to accept it and shoulder it. We'll give everything when we come back to this magnificent stadium on Sunday."

Lens must now regroup quickly before welcoming domestic rivals Marseille back to their home ground in Ligue 1 on Sunday afternoon. Having seen a three-match top-flight winning streak halted by Lille prior to Wednesday's European humiliation, the squad desperately need a response before the November international break. Meanwhile, free-scoring Como have become only the second team to hit nine in a Champions League game after Bayern Munich in September 2024, taking their tally to 19 goals from four matches.

#2790. Bo Nix on the comebacks: ‘We have a lot of guys with a clutch gene’

The Denver Broncos have one 15 consecutive one score games. This is tied for the most all-time. Tying none other than Peyton Manning while he was with the Indianapolis Colts. Even more than that, Bo Nix is averaging a comeback and game winning drive at a rate far beyond anything seen in NFL history.

When asked about his success, Nix believes it goes beyond just one person. He sees the whole team having that clutch gene and that is why they've been so successful.

"I've always felt like I've wanted to feel like a clutch player," Nix said on Wednesday. "It's an important quality as a player when everybody's looking at you and the pressure's on. I don't think you do it individually. If you look at our team in the last three years, we have had 15 game-winning drives. I just think we have a lot of guys with a clutch gene. We have a lot of guys that when the game's on the line, will just find ways to go score. I'd much rather be known as the guy that wins games in the close ones than the guy that always looks great early and can win but doesn't know how to close out the game. I'd much rather be clutch than the other way around."

He's both right and wrong. You need the quarterback more than any other position to have the clutch gene. It feeds the rest. I think back to 2016 and how great that defense was and how clutch they were in 2015. Except, they were not quite clutch enough because the quarterback situation lost its mojo along the way without Peyton Manning's aura around to spark the clutch.

Tim Tebow had it. He was terrible at quarterbacking, but if the game was close everyone on that team believed clutch was going to manifest. It manifested because they all put in the plays to make it happen. It's the same with these Broncos. Bo Nix is the driver. The team is the engine. Together they clutch the heck up week in and week out.

Like John Elway's years. Like Tim Tebow's seven games. Like Peyton Manning's 2015 run. The clutch is a team game, but it needs a quarterback that the players believe can make the magic happen if given the chance.

Bo Nix is that guy too. I am enjoying this ride.

Who needs picks when your offense is lacking?

Every year that passes, I like having draft picks more and more. I fully understand that they are all essentially a roll of the dice, but I'd rather have a bunch of chances at improving the team than not. In general, I'm not normally about trading picks mid-season.

Broncos at Panthers preview: Denver aims to avoid the "trap"

The Broncos head east to face Carolina on Sunday. After a big win and brutal schedule to start, Denver can't let up.

Statistical dive into Denver Broncos record-tying 15th straight win in one-score games

The Denver Broncos have now won 15 straight regular season games that were decided by one-score (8 or fewer points). This ties the 2007-2008 Peyton Manning-led Colts. Since the start of the 2025 season the Broncos are 16 and 2 in one-score games in the regular season (1-1 in the post-season). This is a big change from 2024 when the Broncos were 1-6 in one-score games.

On preparing a gameplan for a team that recently changed defensive coordinators

"I think this: You go by all of the film you have. Really in that first quarter, there may be some things that we see that maybe have changed a little. [It's] hard to change everything in a short period of time. They have a base front and coverage they like to play and then they have a sub package and then it's really more of when they're playing it. Then us being able to in the first quarter see if there's something that's different than we've seen on film."

On if the team is managing RB J.K. Dobbins' workload

"He's a huge part of what we're doing. So each week we look at—a lot of times who's the back that's in there with the hot hand. But he's been fantastic. So to answer your question: No, that's not a hot button topic with us here. It might be with you guys, but not with us. So we're good. We're good with the rotation."

On balancing RB J.K. Dobbins' workload within a three-back rotation

"Oh, we are paying attention to, yes, absolutely. Look, it's always easy to work two (running backs) and it becomes more challenging when you're trying to work three, but he's doing a great job."

"All of that's good. The pressures can lead to interceptions, the sacks can't. So you're looking each week, what quarterback are you defending? We've seen some mobile quarterbacks periodically. Maybe you get a quarterback that you know where they're going to be in the pocket. So I think you have a rush plan based on the offense and who's playing quarterback."

On if opposing offenses have adjusted to the team's pass rush

"Certainly the timing of when you want to throw the ball. There are some quarterbacks that are… Last week, it's hard to sack [Chiefs QB] Patrick [Mahomes]. In other words, he's seen the pressures, he's seen the man… He's got a good clock in his head. So those guys that process fast are difficult. Now fortunately for us, the last play of the game, we were able to get one. I think a lot of it is the offense and the QB. To answer your question, I'm sure there's certain points of emphasis you make relative to the rhythm of your throws if you're seeing a team that rushes the passer well."

"You've definitely seen his ascension, and he's very comfortable with what they're doing. It's an explosive team. I think they're seventh or eighth in explosives. They do a great job mixing the play action, the 'RPO' (Run-Pass Option) game. They've drafted well. So all those numbers are different today than they were two years ago."

On how RB Jonah Coleman has impressed him despite missing time with an injury

"We had those glimpses in the spring and in training camp and in the preseason. Atlanta, there's a run, it just stood out to you. So the one thing that was unique about him is oftentimes you don't get to see them in third down protection plans, but he was someone that we had quite a bit of tape on. Advanced protection plans, and he's built to handle the blitz. It's one thing to know who I have, but then also to be strong enough to do it. I would say that there were three backs—we just saw one of them that we really had visions for. Each one may be a little differently, but his versatility, to your point, that doesn't always—you don't get to stamp that with a lot of rookie backs that you feel like they're going to develop into. We saw enough that we felt like he was going to be a good third down protecting back as well with the way he was built."

On if RB Jonah Coleman has exceeded his expectations in pass protection

"Yeah, he's got good ball skills. We caught him in the right pressure there. Yes, he's very comfortable. He's a different type [of] player than [RB] RJ [Harvey], but there were a lot of traits to like. More importantly, there was the exposure in an offense that sometimes the player just doesn't have that exposure, so you can't know for sure. I think we knew a little bit more with his tape."

On what allows QB Bo Nix to elevate his play when needed

"I don't know. I didn't think he struggled. There's certain…In Seattle, it was the opposite."

On QB Bo Nix's ability to raise his level of play

"I don't have the answer. I know what you're asking. I look at it internally myself like, 'All right, let's get going.' I've said this before, I'll let you know the week we don't want to start fast, but it's not this week. We want to start fast."

On what makes WR Jaylen Waddle dangerous in the low red zone

"He's someone that transitions really quickly. We catch him in a coverage, so he can start and stop and then very quickly outflank leverage, which he did on the one touchdown. I think it was fourth down, but he's got exceptional change of direction."

On the key to building momentum and stringing together wins

"Generally, you have better teams and good teams can… You can't be a yo-yo team and expect to win double digit win. You do the math. So I think what you're asking is the key to building a good football team and that would go all the way back to bringing in the right people, all those things, the right coaching staff and the right culture. Historically speaking, and I'm just going through my experience of having teams that it's hard to win two, lose–it's hard to do that and then turn around and look at the record maybe that you are wanting. Each one of the games is a different type of game. It's like that old boxing analogy. There are certain fights for certain styles and I think that applies a little bit in our game in the NFL."

"I haven't felt it until you just mentioned it. Honestly, I'm being dead serious. I know we had a big win against the Chiefs. I didn't even think how many of that is now. Yes, you're just kind of onto this next one."

"Halftime's eight minutes. We're always on the headsets talking about what's next. You get a chance for a quick message. [The] defense breaks up, offense breaks up, coaches go through real quick, go to your players. It's much quicker. It's much quicker than you could imagine. Every once in a while, there's a game where you get an extra minute, something's going on and then the Super Bowl is entirely different where you can change out your shirts and everything more like hockey. Those guys have kind of a big gap between periods. Ours is like, man… I think you just trust your instincts as to what you just have seen, what you'd like to see in the second half. We're doing this well, let's keep… Then ultimately tune out the scoreboard and just get onto the next play. It's so important. It's so important to not let one play bleed to the next and get onto the next play.

"Oftentimes we as coaches can sit there and be talking about something and it's not going to come up again. So sometimes literally getting onto the next play and knowing you can address that on Monday, or sometimes it is something that could come up again. If it's an offensive play that we've run and if we're spending a bunch of time—we'll get that cleaned up. So back to halftime. No, I'm not yelling or screaming. I had that plan I told you about before the game and the chair was too heavy."

On if a 1 p.m. ET, 11 a.m. MT kickoff changes the team's preparation

"It's new because normally it's been West, and so we'll go out Friday night, get up on their time zone, get a workout, get a little practice in. Then we're kind of going here around Noon. So whatever it is, your spark or your coffee or let's go. So fair question. We studied it and you talk to different people maybe that have been on the West Coast, and we spent time and then finally you have a win at Philly or there's been a few of those and this year we've got… We were hoping to maybe get maybe a couple back-to-back out there, stay out there. It didn't work out that way, but we're not going to Europe. We're going to Charlotte."

On T Garett Bolles' pass protection at left tackle impacting game planning

I know the whole story of the blind side, but you want one of those… In other words, that left tackle, there are times where I'll say to 'Bollesy' (T Garett Bolles), 'Hey, you've got him.' He can do that. Yes, if we're having to make… Now there's times if [Charger OLB] Khalil Mack lines up there, we might move the tight end over there with a Mack protection and just nudge wherever he's at. Last week we had a little protection plan for where [Chiefs DT Chris] Jones was. So I think that's tonight's meeting and it takes a while. Yes, we appreciate the skillset he has."

On if the upcoming Bye Week factors into decisions about players returning from injury

We don't have that luxury. Just 17 games. If he's ready, we treat it like we're playing… That doesn't factor into it at all. It's a good question."

On coordinating with General Manager George Paton at the trade deadline while preparing the gameplan

"We would meet and meet in the evening. The early part of it, all the GMs, they all talk with each other, but he and I'll visit daily. So it's not like it's consuming two hours. On if "spenders" is a term being used around the trade deadline

On if it is difficult to discuss the locker room around the trade deadline

On if the team views itself as a buyer or spender at the trade deadline

On if he considered kicking the chair and if doing so would aggravate his foot

On what changes in the fourth quarter to allow him to have success in those moments

"I don't think anything changes. I just think it's opportunity, and that's just usually how the game goes. It's a one-score game at the end, and you have to go out there and win it."

On balancing winning with team and individual improvement

"Winning's the main goal as a team. There's a process that goes with it. You want to get better yourself. It's really important to win games in this league. On how the offense can stay on the field longer

"I think third-down production would help a lot. I know we're not doing great in that regard. I think that is an area that we can improve."

On how dangerous WR Jaylen Waddle is in short red zone

"I think sometimes it's part of the scheme. He gets some schemed-up plays down there. On the red zone success against the Chiefs and the importance of practicing these situations

"It shows the importance of practice and getting to those over and over. You're right, sometimes you might go through them all (plays). On if he can feel when a young player like RB Jonah Coleman has 'juice'

On the offense's success on two-point conversions and on fourth down

On how the team refocuses after a big win

On how the team refocuses after a big win

On returning to the field last week against Kansas City

"I was very excited to go out there. I was pretty anxious the past three weeks prior to that game. It was fun to get out there with the guys and fly around, make plays. It was a non-contact injury, but the positive news was it was a high ankle sprain, the best news I could get from that. So I just focused on rehab with the trainers and making sure I was able to get back fully to be able to be the best version of myself."

On Head Coach Sean Payton's 200th overall win and the winning culture he has brought to the franchise

"It's great. Obviously Sean, he's brought a winning culture to this organization. It was great seeing that. It was a great milestone for him. Like I mentioned before, he just exudes a lot of confidence, and a lot of confidence and trust in us to be able to get a job done each and every Sunday. Just for him to provide that leadership and each and every week, just preparing us for a new opponent. Just finding ways to get a win is pretty special. So that's a huge accomplishment. We were all happy for him celebrating in the locker room. It was a very special moment."

On what Head Coach Sean Payton has meant to him and how he's helped him elevate his game

"I would say Coach Payton, his first team meeting that he came in, he came in and he kind of set the foundation for his expectations of how he wanted to run the organization, the program—from the players, the behind-the-scenes people, everything. He had a plan. Watching him put that plan into effect, watching him put everything in place, the way that he holds everyone to a standard of what to expect is truly special to be a part of. For him to be the coach, leader, teacher that he is, he always says that his job and the other coaches' jobs aren't just to be coaches; they're there to be teachers. Sometimes it may be about football. Sometimes it may be about life in general. How to become a better young man, man in life. To be able to be around Coach and listen to stories, I find it very humbling and also fascinating to be able to take a step back and just listen to people's stories and the different experiences of life that they've had. For myself, I guess I've been able to play a good amount of time in the league, but Coach has been around the game almost as long as I've been alive. He's seen so many different things. I feel like for myself, to be able to have this humble perspective of this game, being able to listen to Coach talk about the different players that he's been around and coach and just experience, it's really cool to share the locker room with him and to gain as much knowledge as I can because Coach knows a lot of ball. He's been around a lot of ball. He's been around a lot of successful ball, which is why he is the sixth [-fastest] coach to eclipse the milestone he eclipsed on Sunday (200 overall wins). I'm grateful that I get to share the locker room and be around him and learn as much as I possibly can about this game and about life."

On WR Jaylen Waddle getting comfortable in the offense and his performance on Sunday against the Chiefs

"Jaylen has been busting his butt since training camp. He's been putting himself in a position to be able to allow himself and [QB] Bo [Nix] gel as well as they possibly can… Our offense has been working to get to a place of efficiency. To be able to watch him get into the end zone the past couple of times and even the two-point conversion, I think it shows the level of comfort he's [beginning to have] in our offense and us trending that direction of becoming a more efficient and consistent offense."

On what has allowed for QB Bo Nix's 15 career game-winning drives

"I think it's a confidence thing. I think it's a confidence thing in himself, a confidence thing in our offense being able to understand… I think that the more times you get thrown into a situation, the more you're able to overcome said situation. It's like a math problem. The more times you see a math problem, it becomes easier for you to solve that problem when you see it again. I think that us getting thrown into the fire and having to have these comeback moments over the past couple of years and even this year alone, I think that the more you have those opportunities, you see the success and you witness what it's like to have that success. I think there's never a game we feel like we're out of. It doesn't matter how many points we're down. We feel like we have an opportunity to come back and win. You don't want to be in those situations, but when you do have to overcome those situations, having that trump card in your back pocket of saying, 'We've been here before. We know how to win these games. Let's just go out here and do it.' I think that that allows us all to play confident and fast. It's truly special to witness and to be a part of. Like I said, you don't want to be in those situations, but being able to know you can overcome those specific spots in a game is special."

#2789. Joel Embiid hit with technical foul for altercation in 76ers-Pistons

As far as NBA altercations go, this certainly wasn't the most intense. But Philadelphia 76ers star center Joel Embiid drew a technical foul for it, either way.

Embiid and Detroit Pistons forward Tolu Smith engaged in a brief dustup late in the first half of a Wednesday, Nov. 4 game between the two teams.

The play happened with 1:25 left to go in the second quarter, when the 76ers had the ball. Sixers forward Jaylen Brown was driving to the basket when Smith was jostling with Embiid for positioning below the basket. Smith shoved Embiid, who took exception to the move after the play was blown dead.

Embiid then gave Smith a little shove with his right elbow. The contact was minor, but it led to a quick back and forth between the two. It escalated with light shoving, and players eventually had to step in to separate Embiid and Smith, who were shouting and trying to square off.

Eventually, officials reviewed the sequence and levied a technical foul against Embiid for being the one to initiate the action with the elbow.

The Pistons crowd at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit immediately booed Embiid. Pistons All-Star guard Cade Cunningham converted the technical free throw. Embiid was seen encouraging the boos.

The 76ers went on to win 112-106, with Embiid scoring 26 points in the game.

Blue Jays trade idea would bring in All-Star to get back on top of AL East after disappointing season originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

#2784. 76ers star Joel Embiid gets technical foul for shoving match with Tolu Smith in win over Pistons

There were some fireworks with Joel Embiid in the first half at Little Caesars Arena on Wednesday night.

Embiid, who received a technical foul early after a shoving match under the rim, still managed to lead the Philadelphia 76ers to a 112-106 win over the Detroit Pistons. He finished with a double-double with 26 points and 15 rebounds, and powered Philadelphia to an 8-1 record on the year.

But things got heated late in the first half after Jaylen Brown was fouled while shooting under the basket. All of the sudden, as Brown was headed to the free throw line, Embiid got into a shoving match with Detroit's Tolu Smith.

Embiid was jockeying for position with Smith as Brown was working his way to the rim. After the whistle, it looked like Embiid's elbow hit Smith in the chest. Smith then swatted the ball away from Embiid. This led to a shoving match between the two, and in the kerfuffle, Embiid ended up pushing a ref away.

When the dust settled, the refs whistled only Embiid for a technical foul. The Detroit crowd rained down expletives with his last name, and the Philly center stood and egged them on, asking for more.

Pistons point guard Cade Cunningham hit the ensuing free throw from the technical, and Philadelphia went into halftime leading 56-42.

Though the 76ers led by as many as 13 in the final minutes, the Pistons surged late to make it a game. They cut it to just four points after Cunningham hit a layup with 65 seconds left in the contest, but that was as close as they got. Philadelphia held on down the stretch to secure the six-point win.

Embiid shot 8-of-18 from the field and made all 10 of his free throws in the win. The technical was his first of the season. Brown led the way with 30 points and seven assists, and LeBron James finished two assists shy of a triple-double with 13 points, 10 rebounds and eight assists.

Duncan Robinson led the Pistons with 27 points after he went 7-of-11 from the 3-point line. Cunningham had 26 points and 11 assists, and Ausar Thompson had 11 points and 17 rebounds. The Pistons handed the 76ers their lone loss of the season back on Oct. 25. Detroit now sits at 6-2 on the season.

The 76ers and the Pistons will end their three-game season series on February 5.

Embiid has now played in six of the team's games so far this season as the franchise continues to manage his workload to keep him healthy. While things got a bit heated on Wednesday night, Embiid still managed to lift the 76ers to the win without further incident.

#2782. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit

The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman.

Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign.

The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday.

Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship.

"The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box."

Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday.

Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS.

The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then.

Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control.

President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious.

The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants.

Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees.

Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's "The Morning Meeting" podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision.

One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen.

"Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said.

Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC.

In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability.

"If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads."

MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted.

"That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. In conservatorship, the president can do anything."

#2781. Binance breach puts custody at center of crypto infrastructure trade

The $6.3 billion Binance hack could accelerate a shift in how investors value cryptocurrency companies, putting a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to securely hold and protect digital assets.

Much of crypto's evolution this year has involved companies moving past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, to focus instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance. Last Thursday's breach adds a new dimension, bringing cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience into sharper focus.

Importantly, the Binance breach was not an indictment of crypto itself, or a case of leadership-driven fraud, as with FTX in late 2022. Instead, Binance's leadership moved quickly to contain the fallout, protect customers and commit the exchange's own resources to cover losses.

On Tuesday, Binance CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that the company has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.

Management's response, alongside efforts elsewhere in the industry to boost confidence, helped prevent a security breach from escalating into a broader crisis of confidence. For example, Tether, Circle, Ripple and others moved quickly to freeze or restrict access to about $3 billion in stolen assets; Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.

The hack could even help shape the next phase of the crypto infrastructure trade. The new winners may not just be the businesses with the most users, volume or assets under custody, but the ones that can also demonstrate they're able to protect those assets under extreme duress.

"Which company has the resources to invest in cybersecurity and protect customer funds? For a smaller company, it could be much harder because once these crypto companies become infrastructure plays, providing the well for tokenization … they need to have the compliance and control in place so that a similar hacking will not happen or can be minimized," Owen Lau, senior analyst at ClearStreet, told CNBC. "Larger companies have more resources that could give them some advantage."

While institutional investors have increasingly embraced digital assets, broader adoption depends on confidence that those assets can be securely held, accessed and transferred. The Binance breach highlights the importance of that infrastructure, and could increase demand for specialized custodians and platforms with established asset-protection capabilities.

Coinbase has operated a dedicated institutional custody business since 2018. Circle entered the custody business this year, after the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted it approval to operate as a trust bank. In the past few years, Ripple and Kraken have also launched custody businesses.

Still, smaller players compete in the space as well. Small cap crypto exchange stock Gemini Space Station has offered custody services since 2019. BitGo Holdings, founded in 2013, is one of the earliest players in institutional crypto custody and infrastructure, with a reputation for security and serving major institutions.

The shift could also drive consolidation as companies look to buy capabilities, deepen their infrastructure offerings and achieve the scale needed to compete, Lau said.

The more consequential structural shift may be the separation of custody from execution, according to Morgan Stanley.

"Crypto exchanges have historically combined trading, custody, and settlement within vertically integrated platforms, concentrating operational risk. Repeated security breaches could encourage investors to move assets toward independent custody while continuing to trade on CEXs," the firm's analyst Felix Stratmann said in a note Monday," referring to centralized cryptocurrency exchanges.

"This would preserve the role of centralized exchanges as liquidity and execution venues, while potentially benefiting regulated custodians, including banks, as institutional investors place greater emphasis on asset segregation, operational resilience, and investor protection," Stratmann said.

#2780. Former Steelers cornerback announces retirement

Former Steelers cornerback Arthur Maulet is retiring at 33 years old, NFL Network's Cameron Wolfe reported Wednesday evening.

Maulet was an undrafted free agent in 2017 out of Memphis who started his college career at Copiah-Lincoln Community College in Mississippi. In the NFL, the 5'9 cornerback played games for six different teams over his career.

He recorded his most games played (33) and second-most games started (eight) with the Steelers over the 2021 and 2022 seasons after recording 11 total starts with the Jets in 2019 and 2020.

Over his time in the black and gold, Maulet logged 106 total tackles, two sacks, seven tackles for loss, four passes defensed and one interception.

For his career, Maulet played in 94 regular-season games as well as five in the playoffs. After his time with the Steelers, Maulet spent two seasons with the Baltimore Ravens and one with the Detroit Lions.

#2775. Cavs' Jarrett Allen exits early vs. Thunder with right knee injury

Cleveland Cavaliers center Jarrett Allen left Wednesday's matchup with the Oklahoma City Thunder after suffering a right knee injury late in the first quarter.

Allen suffered the injury while setting an off-ball screen just past half-court with the Cavs trailing the host Thunder by 19 points. When Jared McCain tried to get over the screen, the Oklahoma City guard's right knee collided with Allen's right knee, which appeared to jam as he stood rooted to his spot on the floor:

The 11th-year veteran fell to the deck in evident pain, grabbing for that right knee. He laid on the floor for a moment as teammate Mario Hezonja put back an offensive rebound, then raised one finger in the air to signal for a substitution.

After Cavs guard Sam Merrill committed a foul to stop the action, Allen slowly got to his feet and walked gingerly back to the locker room. Shortly thereafter, Cleveland announced that he was doubtful to return to the contest with a right knee injury. When the Cavs came out of the locker room to start the second half, Hezonja took Allen's place in Cleveland's starting lineup alongside Donovan Mitchell, James Harden, Evan Mobley and Tyrese Proctor, whom head coach Kenny Atkinson inserted in place of the injured Peyton Watson.

Allen did not return to Wednesday's game, finishing scoreless with one rebound in seven minutes of playing time. After trailing by as many as 25, the Cavs clawed back to within two possessions several times in the closing minutes. They couldn't get all the way over the hump, though, as the Thunder held on for a 124-116 win behind 42 points and eight assists from two-time NBA MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander.

Allen, 28, has been Cleveland's starting center since joining the team in a trade midway through the 2020-21 season. A one-time All-Star, he's averaging 15.1 points on 63.1% shooting to go with a team-high 8.7 rebounds, 1.7 blocks and 1.4 assists in 27.9 minutes per game for the Cavs, who fell to 4-4 with the loss.

#2774. Nick Bosa returns to practice with limited work

49ers defensive end Nick Bosa returned to practice Wednesday after missing the team's past five games with a calf injury. Bosa was a limited participant.

"It's a long year, and I kind of just reminded myself that I need to be ready for the long haul," Bosa said, via Harrison Rich of the San Francisco Chronicle.

Bosa tore his right ACL in a Sept. 21, 2025, game against the Cardinals and underwent surgery five days later. As he was coming back this summer, Bosa experienced soreness and tendinitis in his right knee, and the 49ers backed him down until Sept. 2 when he returned to practice.

He injured his left calf while warming up in practice for Week 3.

"I must have had some type of compensation going on, especially in that first week back," Bosa said. "I was kind of trying to push it back with the [right knee] tendinitis, so I may have been favoring [the left calf] a little bit. I was just doing my normal warm-up drills one day, and I tweaked it. Calves are a pretty long process. I've never had one, so it took a little longer than I expected, but I don't even think about it anymore."

Wide receiver Mike Evans (ribs/Achilles) remained out of practice, and running back Christian McCaffrey (hamstring) also didn't practice.

Wide receiver Deebo Samuel (hamstring), safety Siran Neal (knee/foot) and offensive tackle Trent Williams (rest) were the other players who sat out Wednesday's session.

Linebacker Luke Gifford (groin), cornerback Nate Hobbs (adductor), wide receiver Christian Kirk (knee), wide receiver Demarcus Robinson (ankle), safety Marques Sigle (ankle), cornerback Upton Stout (shoulder) and linebacker Garret Wallow (hamstring) were limited.

#2773. Mike Vrabel jokes about contractual obligation to meet Tom Brady ahead of Patriots reunion

Mike Vrabel has joked that he is contractually obliged to catch up with Tom Brady when the former New England Patriots quarterback returns to Gillette Stadium for their Week 9 clash with the Green Bay Packers.

Brady is set to be at the Patriots' home ground as a FOX Sports broadcaster, marking a reunion with several familiar faces from his time in New England.

However, Vrabel did not sound particularly enthusiastic when asked whether he would get the chance to meet his former teammate.

Speaking to reporters, the Patriots head coach delivered a playful response when asked about catching up with the seven-time Super Bowl champion.

"I think I'm required contractually to catch up with him at some point," Vrabel said.

He then continued the joke, adding: "I'm sure it'll be a Zoom. I'm sure they won't show up here; I'm sure it will be on Zoom."

Despite the humour, Vrabel made it clear that there was no bad blood between the pair. He described Brady as a friend and said he would "always be a friend", regardless of his professional commitments.

The two spent eight years together in New England, building a relationship during one of the most successful periods in Patriots history.

Vrabel also confirmed that they had exchanged text messages following Super Bowl LX, although they had not met in person.

Their relationship had attracted some attention after Brady said he did not "have a dog" in the Super Bowl between the Patriots and Seattle Seahawks. Some former teammates and fans were reportedly disappointed that he did not openly support New England.

However, Brady's minority ownership stake in the Las Vegas Raiders and his role as a FOX Sports broadcaster meant he had reasons to remain neutral.

Brady, meanwhile, has admitted that returning to Gillette Stadium will be an emotional experience.

"It'll be certainly emotional," he told FOX Sports' Colin Cowherd, reflecting on the memories he made at the stadium.

With Brady back in Foxborough and Vrabel preparing to welcome his former teammate, the Patriots' meeting with Green Bay will offer a reunion that goes beyond the action on the field.

It appears there is a world in which the 49ers could welcome Brandon Aiyuk back with open arms.

As it was reported Tuesday morning, Aiyuk is expected to return to San Francisco's team facility on Friday to be reinstated in the NFL for the first time since December 2025. Shanahan isn't closing the door on a reunion.

San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan is willing to welcome Brandon Aiyuk back with open arms. Getty Images

"There's no absolutes in life, so," Shanahan said to Evan Webeck of the California Post when asked about Aiyuk potentially playing again in a 49ers uniform.

He was asked a follow-up question if he has any concern over the team trading him or releasing him, and potentially playing for a rival team like the Seahawks or Rams, and said, "No."

Aiyuk has been at war with the 49ers for the last year now due to a contract dispute that led to him firing his agent, Ryan Williams of Athletes First.

Over the summer, Aiyuk posted a video on social media calling out Williams and 49ers general manager John Lynch as "weirdos" and "creepy predators" for allegedly showing up at his door.

San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk during team warmups. AP Photo/Jed Jacobsohn

In the video, Aiyuk said his relationship with Shanahan will never be repaired and has no plans on returning to the 49ers' team facility.

It appears that Aiyuk is eating his words and is willing to come back to the facility two days after he hired Drew Rosenhaus as his new agent — who has a plan to get him "back to work and playing again in the NFL."

Shanahan was asked if he heard anything about Aiyuk's reinstatement, and he said he has no expectation.

"I've kind of moved on with that mentally. Kind of how I talked to you guys two months ago. Nothing's really changed for me," Shanahan said.

#2763. Not Hobart, not 183 vs Pak! Virat Kohli names surprising knock as his greatest ever ODI innings on his 38th birthday

Not Hobart, not 183 vs Pak! Virat Kohli names surprising knock as his greatest ever ODI innings on his 38th birthday originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

India ace Virat Kohli has ranked his best ODI knock, and it is not one anyone expected.

A knockout-style contest pitted his hundreds against two quieter innings, with a surprising result.

His logic reveals how he values an innings, and centuries barely feature in it.

MORE: Duffy teases Kohli, calls him 'annoying' after losing 1st ODI at Auckland

Ask most cricket fans to pick Virat Kohli's finest ODI innings and the answer would arrive within seconds, most likely the 183 against Pakistan in Mirpur or the 133 not out in Hobart.

Kohli, who turned 38 today, has chosen neither of them, and his actual pick is a good deal more modest on the scorecard than anything people would have expected.

The batter went through a "winner stays on" exercise in which his memorable innings were set against each other in pairs, and the survivor of each contest moved on to meet a fresh challenger. At the end of the process, the knock left standing was his 43 against England in the 2013 Champions Trophy final at Edgbaston.

What makes the result so striking is the company it beat. Kohli holds the all-time record for ODI hundreds with 55, yet not one of his centuries made it through to the final round, and the innings he valued most were played when a trophy was on the line.

The selection also says something about how he measures his own work. It points to a batter who rates pressure, timing and the outcome of a match above personal milestones, which is an attitude that many modern scorecards, with their emphasis on big numbers, tend to hide.

MORE: Virat Kohli strengthens reputation as ODI cricket's greatest chase master

The challenge began with a contest between the 133 not out against Sri Lanka in Hobart in 2012 and the 35 he made in the 2011 World Cup final at Mumbai. Kohli went with the World Cup knock, even though the Hobart innings involved chasing 321 in just 36.4 overs.

His 35 then held off the 85 against Australia in Chennai in the 2023 World Cup, the 122 against England in Pune in 2017 and the unbeaten 160 against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.

It was only in the fifth round that the 43 from Edgbaston took over, and that innings then beat the 183, the 138 against South Africa and the 107 against Pakistan in Adelaide.

43 vs ENG, Edgbaston, 2013 Champions Trophy final

The final was played on 23 June 2013, and heavy rain cut it down to 20 overs per side, on a damp and tacky pitch that offered generous lateral movement. India lost Rohit Sharma early and were in trouble at 66 for 5 by the 13th over.

Kohli stepped in and top-scored for both teams with 43 off 34 balls, which included four fours and a six, at a strike rate of 126.47. He added 47 with Ravindra Jadeja, who made an unbeaten 33 off 25, and the pair dragged India to 129 for 7.

England were then held to 124 for 8, so India won by five runs and lifted the trophy. That result made MS Dhoni the first captain to win all three major ICC limited-overs trophies.

The innings that held its place for four rounds came on 2 April 2011 in Mumbai, with India chasing 275. Lasith Malinga had Virender Sehwag out for a duck in the first over and removed Sachin Tendulkar for 18, which left the Wankhede in stunned silence at 31 for 2.

The 22-year-old Kohli absorbed the pressure and hit four boundaries in his 35 off 49 balls, a strike rate of 71.42. He put together a vital 83-run stand for the third wicket with Gautam Gambhir, who made 97, before Tillakaratne Dilshan took a brilliant return catch to end his innings at 114 for 3.

The stand steadied the chase and set up Dhoni, who finished on 91 not out, and Gambhir to complete a six-wicket win and India's second ODI World Cup.

Every innings he turned down has its own place in cricket history, which makes the final choice all the more telling.

MORE: Arshdeep Singh remains the clear choice above Siraj in ODIs: Here's why

India had to chase 321 inside 40 overs for a bonus point; Kohli hit Malinga for 24 in an over and finished the job in 36.4 overs.

His career-best ODI score, made in the chase of Pakistan's 329 for 6.

A test of endurance in extreme heat, with 100 runs taken in singles, twos and threes in a total of 303 for 6.

His first match as full-time ODI captain; he added 200 with Kedar Jadhav to rescue India from 63 for 4 in a chase of 351.

It set up a 76-run win in the opener and kept India's unbeaten World Cup record against Pakistan intact.

He rescued India from 2 for 3 in a chase of 200, alongside KL Rahul's 97 not out.

A hundred in testing heat against Steyn, Morkel and Rabada that levelled the series at 2-2.

Kohli's choice will surprise many, yet it fits the kind of cricketer he has become. A man with 55 ODI centuries could easily have picked a big score, and nobody would have complained, but he looked instead at what each innings actually did for the team.

Both of his finalists came under Dhoni in ICC finals, and both ended with India lifting a global trophy. That suggests Kohli sees an innings as valuable only in proportion to what it changed, and a 43 off 34 balls that rescued a side from 66 for 5 is hard to argue against on those terms.

The pick also exposes how poorly raw numbers describe a player's influence. A 183 in a bilateral or continental game will always look bigger in the record books than a 43 in a rain-shortened final, and yet the shorter knock arguably carried far more significance on the day. Strike rates and totals are useful, but they cannot show how much a collapse hurts or how tense a dressing room feels.

There is a lesson here for younger batters as well. Kohli did not wave away his hundreds, and several of them clearly mattered to him, but he was prepared to rank them below two small scores that helped win trophies. On his 38th birthday, that sense of priorities is perhaps the best summary of his career, in which the result has nearly always counted for more than the number beside his name.

#2762. Todd Monken: Deshaun Watson not ruled out yet, but Shedeur Sanders preparing to start

Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson is in the concussion protocol after self-reporting symptoms on Tuesday.

Head coach Todd Monken told reporters in his Wednesday press conference that Watson hasn’t necessarily been ruled out for Sunday’s game against New Orleans. But the club is preparing Shedeur Sanders to start.

“What I would say is, credit to Deshaun — after the game, [he] felt fine. Monday night, started feeling a little bit, little bit of a headache, and came in Tuesday and, you know, reported,” Monken said, via transcript from the team. “So, credit to him for someone who really loves playing the game. And so, he is in the protocol. And Shedeur will take the reps today with the ones.”

Monken admitted that it’s “a little more difficult” for a quarterback to play on Sunday after missing practice due to a concussion. But Monken and the team will let the process play out.

“I mean, there’s a long time between now and then, right? I mean, look where the Ravens are at. And you don’t know as the week goes on what could happen,” Monken said. “It’s not ideal, right? It’s not ideal for any player to go through a week and not practice and then play. We know that. But every situation is different.”

Monken noted that Watson can participate in the team’s meetings to help him stay prepared in the event that he gets cleared. The team has been game-planning with the idea that Sanders will start. But Monken said the game plan won’t change much if it’s Sanders or Watson behind center.

“I don’t see the way [it would change], because the rest of the guys are the same, and they’re similar in some ways,” Monken said. “Some things, you know, Shedeur’s skill set is different than Deshaun’s, but still very similar in terms of what we do. We can’t change that dramatically.”

Either way, Watson is expected to still be the starter when he is cleared.

“Yeah, I didn’t assume I’d get that question. Yeah, he’s been our starter for eight games. I would assume he’s still our starter,” Monken said. “I don’t — I’m thinking about Wednesday. But I’m not — I’m really thinking about today and watching Shedeur play today.”

So far this season, Watson has completed 65.5 percent of his passes for 1,806 yards with seven touchdowns and three interceptions. He’s been sacked a league-high 33 times. His eight games this season are the most he’s played in a year for the Browns since arriving on the club in 2022.

Last season, Sanders completed 56.6 percent of his throws for 1,400 yards with seven touchdowns and 10 interceptions in eight games with seven starts.

When 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan was asked in September if the team’s injury issues at wide receiver had led him to consider bringing Brandon Aiyuk back, his answer was a strong no.

Aiyuk has started the process of being reinstated from the team’s reserve/left squad list and part of that process would involve him reporting to the team’s facility later this week if he has not been released ahead of time. Shanahan was asked at a Wednesday press conference about any expectations he has about such a visit.

“None. I have no expectation,” Shanahan said. “I’ve kind of moved on with that mentally and doing kind of how I talked to you guys two months ago. Nothing’s really changed for me.”

Shanahan said he has not had any conversations about a roster exemption that would give the 49ers more time to explore a trade, which joins releasing him or welcoming him back to the active roster as the team’s options once he is off the left squad list. Shanahan said there are “no absolutes” when asked if he could envision any scenario where Aiyuk plays for the team again, but his other answers sent a strong message that Aiyuk will be moving on once the administrative work is done.
