#2649. Why Yaxel Lendeborg could be the key to saving what's left of the Warriors' Stephen Curry era

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After Yaxel Lendeborg decided to start a war of words with Luka Dončić both during and after his first NBA game last week --more or less calling one of the best players in the world a crybaby for whom he "lost all respect" -- both Stephen Curry and Steve Kerr remarked that they were fine with the don't-give-a-damn brashness of the Warriors' rookie. Curry and Kerr even said that they liked it, but with the caveat that he would, of course, have to "back it up."

How's that going so far? Well, put it this way: If Lendeborg keeps playing like this, the only other thing he's going to have to back up is a Brinks truck to collect his next contract. Through his first five games, the No. 11 overall pick is averaging 22.6 points, 9.6 rebounds and four assists.

Those are not just All-Star numbers. Those are historic numbers. Let's break them down.

Let's start with the basics: Lendeborg is the first Warriors rookie since Stephen Curry to score at least 25 points in three straight games. That's more of a footnote considering Golden State's many draft whiffs over the last 15 years, but still, this is no easy feat over any three-game rookie stint, let alone inside the first two weeks of your career.

Players to record at least: 100 PTS, 40 REB, 20 AST in their first five career games:— Larry Bird— Yaxel LendeborgThat’s it. That’s the list. pic.twitter.com/chE6N6kE1v

Putting up these kinds of numbers can only happen, one, if you've got the game, but two, and in the context of the Warriors this may be the even more important part, if you're given the opportunity to do so. Which brings us to ...

This is no small feat. Maybe it's because he's an old rookie. He's 23. Spent six years in college. Started at a junior college. Grinded through every level and has the maturiity in both game and mind to show for it.

This is important, because it would be easy to classify Lendeborg as immature for all his spouting off, but much like Draymond, listen to what he's actually saying rather than how or to whom he's saying it. Before you go off in judgment of a man with an opinion, understand that he's earned his maturity in ways that, frankly, a guy like Dončić hasn't.

Luka was a prodigy from Day 1, and was treated as such. That isn't a shot at Luka. It's just the reality. Yaxel has worked real jobs in the real world. He didn't even play sports when he first got to high school. He was trying to make money in the same warehouse in which his mom worked.

Imagine hating on a guy who used to work a 9-5 Warehouse Job and now drops 26/8 in the league pic.twitter.com/jopnOFjHnJ

Don't confuse Yaxel having strong opinions with being a know-it-all. The smartest players, and people, seek wisdom, and Yaxel has talked repeatedly about sponging off Curry and Green. After putting up 31 points, 12 rebounds and six assists against Denver, he used his postgame interview with ESPN's studio show to solicit advice from Vince Carter, Carmelo Anthony and Tracy McGrady.

I take great pride in my cynicism, and normally this kind of platform pandering would trigger all the eye-rolling alarms, but Lendeborg appears to be so authentic that you honestly believe he's asking the greats for tips on national television because he actually wants the tips.

When Yaxel talked about the league being full of floppers, the part that didn't get circulated was him saying he is going to learn all the tricks to take "as many free throws as possible." Even when he's criticizing something, he's clocking it, too. This is a clearly an observant and, contrary to the trash-talking perceptions, humble guy who has spoken about wanting to leave Kerr with the impression of "someone who's willing to learn" and hold himself to a standard worthy of a championship coach's trust.

For instance, you may think putting up 26 points and nine boards in your fifth career game, as Lendeborg did in a win over the Wolves on Wednesday, is a great showing, but Lendeborg described his performance as "hella soft" while lamenting a "timid" approach that led to him committing seven turnovers.

Kerr has noted that Lendeborg needs to improve his weak-side defensive focus, that he can run the floor harder, and that he tried to "force a lot of plays" against Minnesota (Kerr has talked about sometimes it being as simple as taking one more dribble before taking to the air on a drive), which was a point he made after Lendeborg went for 26 points, nine rebounds and five assists against Phoenix.

Steve Kerr mentioned after the Phoenix game that Lendeborg needed to get more creative when attacking the shot blocker. Pump fake, jump stop, euro step, kick-out pass, you name it.Multiple times in his first three games, Lendeborg launched himself into the rim protector and got… pic.twitter.com/gKndrpU9bd

This is a fine line for a 6-foot-9, 250-pound "strong as an ox" guy who butters a lot of bucket-getting bread with power drives. Draymond is telling Yaxel to go through defenders' chests, while Kerr is telling him to him to slow down, see the floor and make sound decisions without compromising aggression.

There's nuance and interpretation in both those messages, and surely this is the stuff that Kerr, Green, Curry and all the other Golden State vets are going to be talking with Yaxel about all year. Mistakes are sometimes the most important ingredient in a developmental stew. That's where the learning comes from, and Yaxel is certainly going to travel a steep curve on his way to finding his strength-skill sweet spot, particarly within the context of a team that needs him to make things happen.

Somewhere Jonathan Kuminga is surely wondering why he was never afforded the luxury of playing through his mistakes, while Lendeborg is crashing into defenders and committing 18 turnovers over his last four games and still leading the team in minutes.

To that, allow me to summon my inner-Yaxel and not beat around the bush with this one: He's worlds better than Kuminga (who never embraced or more importantly improved upon any part of the game other than scoring) ever was for the Warriors. And besides that, Kuminga wasn't, and isn't, the non-interruptive scorer that Lendeborg has already showed himself to be anyway, to say nothing of all the other basketball boxes he checks.

You can see the whole Yaxel package in this reel below. The bully, through-the-chest drives and a deceleration finish that speaks to the composed attacks Kerr wants to see more of. The spot-up shooting (8 of 12 from 3 so far on these shots, per Synergy). The chase-down block on one end into a floor-running finish on the other. The athletic cuts. The savvy pick-and-roll feel (watch him smoothly split the defenders at the 1:25 mark). Pay close attention to the way Yaxel spins into the lane for a finish on Nikola Jokić at the 16-second mark, and then, later, how he makes the same move but this time the defense collapses and he recognizes it immediately and zips a pass to the corner for a Brandin Podziemski 3.

Yaxel WENT OFF in Golden State's win 🔥31 PTS (career-high)12 REB (game-high)6 ASTHe becomes the first @warriors rookie since Steph Curry (2/10/2010) to record 30+ PTS, 10+ REB, and 5+ AST in a single game! pic.twitter.com/FYe42bFtD8

Kerr has called Lendeborg "100%" the most pro-ready rookie that he's ever coached, noting that he knew Lendeborg had the shoot-pass-dribble skill package to be effective right away, but that he also "has a better feel for the game than I realized." That's why Kerr trusts him to not just be on the floor more than any other player so far, but to actually pilot an offense that is registering a top-five rating during his minutes, per Cleaning the Glass.

"Basically, at all the critical moments of the game, we just put the ball in his hands," Kerr said after that Denver game. "For a rookie to be that advanced already, it's extremely rare."

Long term, Lendeborg looks like the next-era star that Joe Lacob has been desperate to land since the start of the decade, which he seemingly thought was the beginning of Curry's end. Lacob was extremely wrong about that, and this ownership has been wrong about damn near every draft pick it has made over the last eight-plus years.

The 2020 and 2021 drafts, in particular, were supposed to set up Golden State's future, and they became the basis for the ill-fated two-timeline plan. The organization was too slow, or stubborn, or probably both, to ditch that plan and trade some of those guys while they still had some value.

Wiseman and Kuminga basically were given away. Moody has been a fine rotation guy, ho-hum by lottery pick standards, while Brandin Podziemski, taken with the 19th pick in 2023, has been solid (don't listen to the idiots who say Podz has been a disaster; it's not even close to true). But those players are not home runs.

Even at 23 years old, Yaxel looks like a home run. And beyond what this means for Golden State's long-term outlook, it begs the question of whether he changes the short-term plans for a front office that had seemingly conceded to a lost season as it gears up for a 2027 cap-space splurge.

Is Lendeborg really good enough already to make the Warriors think they are a piece away from contention? Bill Simmons seemed to suggest as much when he recently declared that "Yaxel might have single-handedly saved the Steph era" while comparing him to 2010s LeBron James.

If you audibly laughed at a prime-LeBron comp, you're not alone. But it speaks to the kind of buzz Lendeborg is generating, and the Warriors are definitely feeling it, too. Might they look at trading, say, Draymond Green, who's on an expiring contract? Perhaps they could pair Green with Kristaps Porzingis, who's only guaranteed $3 million next season, for close to $50 million in trade value.

Add some draft equity to that package, and you can go hunting for some pretty big game. What about Trey Murphy III. What about adding Moody in and going after Anthony Davis? Imagine a Warriors team with Curry, who's still playing at an All-NBA level, Yaxel and a third All-Star to be named, with Jimmy Butler still coming back. Or you could trade Butler with some draft picks and do any of the same things.

Before Yaxel shot out of a cannon, the Warriors seemed way too far away from even fringe contention to justify an all-in trade. You can argue they've been too focused on the blockbuster trades at the expense of the more peripheral moves that could've kept Curry competitive, like the ones the Knicks made for OG Anunoby (who, incidentally, was another Warriors "target") and Mikal Bridges, and Yaxel, in his career infancy, feels like that caliber of player. Not a star (yet), but a guy who can provide contention-level star support. Maybe the Steph Curry doesn't have to die on the vine after all.

Bear in mind, the Warriors would have to trade draft picks to make anything happen, and for all the fans who love to mortgage the future, remember, this summer there were a lot of people who wanted the Warriors to trade the No. 11 pick with which they drafted Yaxel. So be careful what you wish for.

That said, they got Yaxel. The Warriors have been wrong about a lot in post-Kevin Durant era, but all signs point toward them being absolutely right about Lendeborg. And now that they have him, it's fair to wonder if he covers enough of their future to actually start trying to maximize their present.

#2648. 'It was about each other': The Brewers and Pat Murphy admire the masterpiece they built

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Construction requires purpose.

Before materials are collected. Before architects render blueprints. Before the site gets chosen. There must be vision. The building of something, anything monumental, is less about machinery and labor. But about inspiration. It's the ultimate binding force. Human ingenuity powered by a bent for progress, a hope for excellence.

It's the purpose that fuels the willingness to build. And shared purpose produces the buy-in.

The work in progress that was the Brewers, a project eight years in the making dating back to Christian Yelich's arrival in 2018, was finally ready for the ultimate ribbon-cutting on Wednesday night at Tropicana Field. An unveiling of their finished work.

It took just five games to deconstruct the Rays. But it took eight years to build a team worthy of this moment.

And it took the Brewers 57 years to find the right construction workers to deliver the franchise's first-ever World Series championship.

"They decided to be uncommon," manager Pat Murphy told CBS Sports following his team's 4-1 Game 5 win. "And when they made that decision that it was about each other — when it's about each other and it's a team, you can accomplish anything."

Yelich, the 34-year-old captain, is at the center of all of this. He arrived in Milwaukee in 2018 and quickly became an MVP that season. A name that offered a glimmer of what the future could be. The Brewers made it to the NLCS that first year with Yelich, falling one game shy of a World Series trip.

Yelich was the ultimate building block for a club in dire need of one. He became the franchise. And the Brewers became perennial contenders, making the playoffs in every season with Yelich except 2022.

When the legs grew a little heavier with age. When the swing slowed. When the five tools became four, then three, then two. When the player who once carried a franchise had to learn what it meant to be carried by one.

His playing time dwindled. He didn't say a word.

Matchups against lefties began casting doubt over whether his name would appear on the lineup card. He didn't say a word.

And now, playing more of a supportive than a starring role, he's a World Series champion.

"It's an awesome feeling, man," he said, "and just so happy for our team, our city, all the guys, man. It's just it's the best feeling ever."

A man who has traveled a long road. You hear it in his voice. In his perspective. There's failure in it.

He spent a quarter-century as a college coach, most notably at Arizona State, where he was among the premier coaches in the sport. Much like Pat Casey at Oregon State, now also on the Brewers' staff, or Augie Garrido at Cal State Fullerton, Murphy was the kind of coach high school players dreamed of playing for.

But an NCAA investigation in 2009, one that ultimately cleared Murphy of unethical conduct but found fault with his oversight of the program, brought his college coaching career to an abrupt end.

And even after all of that, Murphy, drenched in champagne amid the lingering aroma of cigars, admitted something dumbfounding.

"I wasn't a very good coach," he said. "I had a lot of wins maybe."

Murphy joined the Padres as a special assistant. He managed the Eugene Emeralds, Tucson Padres and El Paso Chihuahuas. He even managed the Padres themselves on an interim basis before joining the Brewers in 2015 as bench coach under Craig Counsell, his former player at Notre Dame.

The teacher had to become a student again.

"There was so much I had to grow," he said.

There's David Hamilton, who returned to the organization that drafted him after a stint with the Red Sox. In Boston, he lost his way. His confidence disappeared. The game looked too fast for one of baseball's fastest players. The Red Sox tried to change him, encouraging him to pull the ball in the air, much as they do with many of their hitters. But it didn't work.

So when he returned to Milwaukee, Murphy had a message for him: Hit more ground balls to the opposite field. Bunt more.

"Really just trying to get on base," he said. "I think getting on base ultimately helps the team win."

There's Jake Bauers, a man who once considered retirement amid his struggles, now a World Series champion.

"It all changed for me when I realized it wasn't about me," he said.

There's Sal Frelick, the overlooked, undersized glue guy who, according to his manager, might have broken his hand after being hit by a pitch in Game 5. But Murphy trusted him to stay in the game.

"I said, when this last out is recorded and we're the last man standing, Sal Frelick will be on the field. That's just because of who he is," Murphy said.

Catcher William Contreras required a different kind of work.

Pet him, and he just might nip you, according to Murphy.

But that doesn't mean Murphy is afraid to put his paws on him.

He benched Contreras at the end of September for failing to hustle down the first-base line.

It was done with love. Murphy leads with love, but never at the expense of discipline. And with Contreras, he came to understand something else.

"The ones that are toughest to love need the love the most," Murphy said. "And he's a guy that needs the love, and it has to be real."

Contreras went on to put together one of the best postseasons in recent memory, becoming World Series MVP.

Champagne and beer filled the visitors' clubhouse. The cramped quarters were an afterthought amid the joy engulfing the room. The smell of victory permeated the air. The speakers boomed. The Game's "Hate It or Love It" blared over the sound system.

"Hate it or love it, the underdog's on top."

The Brewers, undoubtedly, were the underdogs. Despite winning 97 games the previous season, preseason projections pegged them for roughly 80 to 84 wins.

They traded Freddy Peralta to the Mets. Their rotation leaned heavily on young arms: Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and Kyle Harrison, alongside an aging, oft-injured Brandon Woodruff.

They found a Cy Young Award winner in Misiorowski, the premium talent with a 105-mph fastball. Misiorowski tossed 5⅓ scoreless innings. Even without his typical swing-and-miss stuff, the right-hander limited the Rays to just two hits.

"This is crazy," a wide-eyed Misiorowski said on the field.

Because the Brewers have repeatedly found ways to survive the departures of players who once seemed indispensable. Josh Hader. Corbin Burnes. Devin Williams. Even manager Craig Counsell and former president of baseball operations David Stearns.

Yet Milwaukee, steered by Matt Arnold, who succeeded Stearns as president of baseball operations following the 2023 season, has continued to scout, draft and develop talent. Many of the anchors of this championship team were homegrown: Cooper Pratt, Jackson Chourio, Misiorowski, Brice Turang, Aaron Ashby, Abner Uribe, Garrett Mitchell, Frelick, Luis Lara and Henderson.

"We invest a lot of minutes in acquisition and development," Arnold said. "We've got to make sure that pipeline is very strong. That's our foundation."

Many have tried. Few have done it like Milwaukee.

Murphy stepped back onto the field early Thursday morning as a champion. The sea of Brewers fans that had overtaken Tropicana Field all week made their presence known. They chanted his name. They cried. Together. Because it had been a long time.

The cheers grew louder. The smiles wider. The cries more profound.

Murphy stopped. Soaking in his organization's creation. A vision realized. Something built, not bought.

"I needed them more than they needed me," he said of his players.

And yet, the Brewers aren't finished. A project eight years in the making still has work to do, much like the people who helped build it.

"We're always under construction," Murphy said.

#2646. Three reasons why the Brewers can repeat as World Series champions in 2027

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Brewers are the freshly crowned World Series champions for 2026. Add that trophy to a regular season body of work in which they won 103 games and achieved the best run differential in all of Major League Baseball, and it's clear the Brewers this season did all a team can do. The first title in franchise history will be remembered and cherished by the Brewers and their fans forever, and it was earned in every respect.

The celebrations won't soon end, and the post-Game 5 hangovers are still pulsing. Even so, it's time to turn our attention to the 2027 season and explore why the Brewers absolutely have the foundation necessary to do it all again next year. Here, then, are three reasons the Brewers can become repeat champions roughly one year from now.

Eyeball the Brewers' current contract obligations and service time tiers, and you'll find just six players are likely bound for free agency. Brandon Woodruff, Jake Bauers, JoJo Romero, and Gary Sánchez will be free agents soon. Elsewhere, Dustin May has a mutual option for 2027, which means he'll probably join them. Finally, Antonio Senzatela has a $14 million team option for 2027 on which the Brewers may pass.

Of those, the 31-year-old Bauers is the biggest needle-mover, as he's coming off a 2026 season in which he hit 26 home runs in 144 games and put up a WAR of 3.3. He does seem likely to move on, but the Brewers are more than resourceful enough to find comparable production from the non-premium position of first base.

Elsewhere, the Brewers should resist the temptation to trade away catcher, linchpin, and reigning World Series MVP William Contreras ahead of his walk year in 2027. The Brewers Way in recent years has been to part ways with core contributors around such a time, and that may be a temptation with Contreras, especially given Bo Naylor's presence on the roster. Contreras, though, is not easily replaceable given his skills behind the mask and his high level of production at the plate. An extension may not be something the Brewers will pursue – even though the ongoing CBA negotiations will probably lead to a new system that benefits teams like Milwaukee – but even if that's the case, they should keep their catcher and leader around for the final year of team control in the name of defending the belt and the title.

The champion Brewers, as a club that gets limited investment from ownership and is elite at player development, skews young even as they stand as the best team in baseball. Consider:

As for specific examples, they're not hard to find. Budding star Jackson Chourio will be in his age-23 campaign in 2027. Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson will each be 25. Cooper Pratt, like Chourio, will be 23. The Brewers this past season got 16.4 WAR from those names, and Pratt and Henderson didn't even log full seasons.

Let's also note that Brice Turang, who led the Brewers this season with a WAR of 7.3, will be just 27 in '27 and thus should continue performing at a high level. This isn't just a matter of the Brewers being largely shielded from age-related decline next season. There's also the distinct possibility that so many of their 2026 pace-setters are still pre-prime and may have even better days ahead.

As though all of the above weren't enough, the Brewers right now have managed to thread this rare needle: they're the best team at the highest level and have one of the best collections of talent down on the farm. MLB.com in August ranked the Brewers as the third-best farm system in the game right now. FanGraphs ranked them third based on average prospect value. Baseball America at midseason likewise ranked the Milwaukee system third and after the season gave the system an "A" grade.

At an individual level, a number of premium Brewers prospects figure to arrive at some point next season. That list includes shortstop Jesús Made, who may be the top prospect in the game right now. Other 2027 arrivals may include talents like corner infielder Andrew Fischer, right-handers Tyson Hardin and Bishop Letson, and infielder/outfielder Jett Williams, among others. So many teams in contending mode have a fairly dry pipeline thanks to the low draft picks and the now-for-later trades that often accompany World Series aspirations, but that's very much not the case with lead executive Matt Arnold and the Brewers.

Celebrations of the work done in 2026 should be the focus right now for the Crew and their rooters, and once that dies down, they can all be further buoyed by the reality that the Brewers aren't going anywhere. The guess here is that the Brewers open the 2027 season – whatever it looks like — as the consensus favorites to do it all again.

#2644. Top 25 MLB trade candidates for 2026-27 offseason: Paul Skenes, Jeremy Peña and more who could move

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the Milwaukee Brewers crowned as the 2026 World Series champions, the 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is now upon us.

While the arc, pace, and even length of this offseason are all uncertain thanks to the ongoing CBA negotiations, we do know that at some point before the next season begins, we'll have a flurry of free agent signings and trades. The focus in this space right now is on the latter: possible winter trades.

We're about to examine the 25 leading trade candidates of the offseason. Obviously, this won't be an exhaustive list of players who might be traded, and just as obviously not all of these names to come will be on the move. Some, though, will, and all of these names have been deemed as distinct possibilities based on reporting, service time and payroll considerations, and prior organizational decision-making.

We'll explore names by putting them in groups based on the underlying reasons or causes of their status as trade candidates. Here are those groups:

The 25 names to come won't be ranked, but instead will be listed alphabetically within their respective categories. Now let's get to it.

Duran's taken a serious fall from the heights of 2024, when he earned an All-Star selection and cracked the top 10 of the American League MVP vote. He cratered last season, which makes this winter something of an inopportune time to trade him from the Boston standpoint. That said, the Red Sox have a crowded outfield with Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Roman Anthony, which means a Duran swap may be needed to clear the decks. If nothing else, the 30-year-old outfielder presents a buy-low/change-of-scenery opportunity for a team looking to take a risk.

Potential fits: Phillies, Cubs, Mariners, Rangers

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 50%

Hernández has been a reliable power presence for the Dodgers, but now, at age 34, he's been showing some signs of decline. On another level, the Dodgers want to make space for elite prospect Josue De Paula to receive regular playing time, and there aren't any other paths to it. That may mean Hernández will be on the move.

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 45%

Kwan's another who's been a reliable presence in the trade rumors for some time. Cleveland also has a history of dealing core talents leading up to their walk year, and Kwan is indeed slated for free agency after next season. The timing would be right, as Kwan is coming off a 5.0-WAR season for the second time in his career.

Potential fits: Phillies, Blue Jays, Cubs, Mariners

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 30%

McClanahan's long and labored comeback from Tommy John surgery was finally realized this past season, and he turned in a strong age-29 campaign for the Rays. These, though, are the Rays, and McClanahan's forthcoming arbitration payday combined with his uncertain health history may prompt them to shop him to pitching-starved fellow contenders. He carries risk, of course, but there will no doubt be potential takers lining up for him.

Potential fits: Braves, Padres, Orioles, Tigers

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 35%

Thanks to a blazing fastball and wipeout knuckle curve, the soon-to-be 33-year-old Megill has been a lockdown closer for most of the last three seasons. The Brewers of course have a substantial history of trading away closers before they reach their high-salary years and also before they regress/decline (see: Hader, Josh and Williams, Devin). That could again be the case with Megill, who'll be in line for free agency after the 2027 season.

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 55%

He's the most dominant closer in baseball and the owner of one of the biggest fastballs ever, and he's under team control through the 2029 season. So why would the contending Padres trade Miller at the peak of his powers? They'd consider doing so because they have a lot of roster holes to fill elsewhere, especially with Michael King opting out of his contract. Trading away Miller would in theory allow them to fill some of those holes, which is why it'll be a temptation for lead executive AJ Preller. No doubt, fellow contenders will be lining up if the Pads do indeed shop the NL saves leader.

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 20%

Strider not so long ago was in the discussion for most dominant starter in the bigs, but persistent arm woes have turned him into a question mark. The Braves came close to dealing Strider at the deadline in exchange for more of a known quantity in the rotation, so there's basis for his inclusion on this list. Any team acquiring him will have to be comfortable with Strider's medicals and the fact that he's owed a minimum of $49 million over the next two seasons. His ace upside, though, is surely tantalizing.

Potential fits: Cardinals, Padres, Orioles, Tigers, Dodgers

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 25%

The Nats were clear sellers at the deadline, but they retained Abrams, who has two full years of team control remaining. In other words, it's going to take a lot to pry him away. At 26, he's coming off a 30-30 season, and he's been a quite productive bat over the last three years. Defensively, Abrams probably isn't an everyday shortstop moving forward, but second base is now in his toolkit.

Potential fits: Braves, Pirates, Red Sox, Giants, Rangers

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 25%

Teams will pay a lot for a young and controllable starting pitcher with frontline upside, and all of that describes the 27-year-old lefty Detmers. Not eligible for free agency until after the 2028 season, Detmers topped 4.0 WAR this past season and struck out 211 batters in 185 innings. For the Halos, trading him might be an example of selling high.

Potential fits: Cardinals, Red Sox, Cubs, Blue Jays, Padres

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 30%

As a 27-year-old All-Star catcher with three full seasons of team control remaining, Goodman would cost a lot in trade. Perhaps that's why the rebuilding Rockies will indeed deal him this winter. There's no doubt that playing his home games in Coors Field helps Goodman's cause, but this past season, he was actually much more productive on the road. Away from Coors, he hit 25 of his 41 home runs in 2026, and his road slugging percentage was .564 versus a .490 figure at a mile above sea level. That's power that will play anywhere.

Potential fits: Giants, White Sox, Yankees, Orioles

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 50%

Greene has one of the biggest fastballs in the game and a top 10 finish in the NL Cy Young balloting in his recent past. However, he's struggled to stay healthy and realize his potential on a sustained basis – the potential that made him the No. 2 overall draft pick in 2017. He's signed through 2028 with a club option for 2029, and it may be time for a change of scenery. He's been the subject of trade speculation before.

Potential fits: Dodgers, Braves, Red Sox, Astros, Blue Jays

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 25%

Herrera is not a particularly skilled defensive catcher outside of blocking pitches in the dirt, but he can get by behind the mask, at least on a part-time basis. He also has a plus bat, which will play at DH or perhaps first base and even left field. The Cardinals have an incoming glut of catchers, which means it may be time to move on from Herrera. He's not eligible for free agency until after the 2029 season.

Potential fits: Yankees, White Sox, Orioles, Giants

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 30%

The Marlins seem likely to trade away one of their middle infielders this winter, either the shortstop Lopez or second baseman Xavier Edwards. For now, we'll focus on Lopez, who would likely fetch the higher return. The 28-year-old Lopez this past season topped 6.0 WAR, led the NL in hits, and swiped 34 bases, all while grading out as a valuable defender at the premium position of short. He's under team control through the 2029 season, which means he'll have immense trade value.

Potential fits: Braves, Phillies, Red Sox, Rays

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 20%

The most underrated player in baseball? The 25-year-old Neto is very much in that discussion. Over the last three seasons, he's amassed a WAR of 15.6, which puts him in elite territory. Any team in need of excellence and stability on the left side of the infield should have interest. Neto isn't eligible for free agency until after the 2029 season, which adds to his already substantial trade value.

Potential fits: Braves, Red Sox, Tigers, Cardinals, Yankees

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 30%

No, this one isn't likely to happen, as Contreras has proved central to the Brewers' success in 2026 and for years prior. That said, the ever-resourceful Brewers do have a ready replacement on the roster in Bo Naylor. The 2026 World Series MVP is also in line for free agency after the 2027 season, which theoretically increases the chances that Milwaukee will explore his trade market. Speaking of which, such a skilled catcher with a potent bat and reputation as a leader will indeed have a healthy market.

Potential fits: Yankees, Rangers, Orioles

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 15%

For years now, it seems, we've been waiting for the Mariners to trade from their surfeit of starting pitching. They moved Luis Castillo at the deadline, but perhaps this time, they finally flip one of their big guns. Gilbert, 29, will be a pending free agent in 2027, which straightaway makes him a trade candidate for a Mariners club that's more averse to spending than they should be. He's an attractive one, too, as Gilbert has been a reliable source of innings over his career to date, and he also boasts a 3.58 FIP and a sparkling 5.14 K/BB ratio over the last four seasons.

Potential fits: Mets, Braves, Orioles, Cubs, White Sox

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 45%

Paredes, who turns 28 in February, is on a $13.35 million team option for 2027, and then he's eligible for free agency. That adds up to the real possibility of a trade out of Houston. While there are questions as to how Paredes' bat will play without the Crawford Boxes near at hand, there's no doubt he's overall a valuable performer. He's fresh off a 4.0-WAR season in 2026 and relatively young as notable trade targets go.

Potential fits: Phillies, Cardinals, Yankees

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 45%

Peña, like Paredes, will be a pending free agent in 2027, and the increasingly incompetent Astros may look to trade him as they did Kyle Tucker back in the winter of 2024-25. Peña, 29, hasn't been especially durable over the last two seasons, but when on the field, he remains an excellent all-around performer. If he is indeed shopped, then he's the most appealing shortstop on the trade and free agent markets this offseason.

Potential fits: Braves, Red Sox, Phillies

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 35%

Ryan has been the subject of trade speculation for what feels like the last half-decade. Has the time finally come for those rumors to be realized? Now 30, Ryan will be a free agent after the 2027 season, and that of course means he could be on the move this winter. He has excellent stuff, and over the last three seasons Ryan boasts an ERA+ of 117 and a K/BB ratio of 5.38.

Potential fits: Cubs, Astros, Mets, Orioles, Red Sox, Blue Jays

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 35%

Yes, deGrom is 38, but going into the final guaranteed year of his contract, he remains capable of being a solid rotation presence for a contender. deGrom reportedly used his full no-trade clause to block a trade to the Braves at the deadline, so it's far from certain whether he'd be willing to approve a deal out of Arlington. That said, such things are always negotiations, and a late-career run at the playoffs might prove tempting for him.

Potential fits: Braves, Dodgers, Blue Jays

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 25%

The future Hall of Famer is coming off another solid season once you consider that a spring hamate injury likely sapped his production early on. That said, he soon turns 33, and he's still owed $160 million through 2031. That's in addition to his full no-trade clause. The Mets and Lindor, though, may be at a crossroads in their relationship, which makes it at least theoretically possible that a change of scenery is in the offing.

Potential fits: Braves, Mariners, Phillies

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 15%

Marte already had a partial no-trade clause in his contract, which runs through 2030 (with a 2031 player option), and now he's earned a full no-trade clause through 10-and-5 rights. That said, after multiple somewhat bizarre AWOL incidents with the D-backs, Marte and the club may be looking for a fresh start. While Marte's offensive outputs dipped last season, his age-32 campaign, he still profiles as at least an above-average player for the near- to mid-term. And he may be more than that if he gets back to something like his pre-2026 peak.

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 30%

Now 32, Seager will always have health and durability concerns, but he remains a plus defensive shortstop who produces well at the plate by positional standards. With the Rangers perhaps looking to shed payroll, they could seek to move Seager, who's owed another $155 million through the 2031 season. As with the Mets and Lindor, that may mean kicking in cash to make a trade happen, but Seager would help the cause for any contender in need of help at the shortstop position.

Potential fits: Braves, Mariners, Phillies

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 20%

Will the increasingly listless Reds pivot toward a longer-term rebuild? If they do, then their electric 24-year-old shortstop could be dangled. De La Cruz is coming off his best season to date, and there's the feeling that he still has offensive upside in the tank. He's under team control through the 2029 season. Those three full years of control plus De La Cruz's MVP upside mean we'd be talking about a true blockbuster of a trade. No, it's not particularly likely to happen, but it's an intriguing possibility.

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 15%

This is becoming something of an annual exercise in speculation and wish-casting (wish-casting by non-Pirates fans, anyway). Skenes took a step back last season in terms of run prevention and underlying indicators, and he also lost a bit off his fastball. Still, he was overall a high-value pitcher who still projects as an ace, and he's not far removed from those legendary rookie and sophomore seasons. Like De La Cruz above, Skenes has three more full seasons before free agency, which makes his trade value pretty well stratospheric. The Pirates aren't likely at all to move him, particularly ahead of a new CBA that may benefit teams of their sort, but the Skenes trade conjecture isn't going anywhere.

With the World Series complete and the book closed on the 2026 MLB season, it's just about time for the Hot Stove. This offseason will be defined by collective bargaining negotiations between MLB and the MLBPA, and the nearly certain lockout that seems destined to begin in December casts a ton of uncertainty over free agency. But players will move at one point or another. So who's on the market? We ranked the top 50 free agents.

The No. 1 available player is no secret. If you follow baseball even somewhat closely, you probably know that Tarik Skubal is the biggest prize. Expect the top World Series contenders to be in play for his services. Behind him is a mix of reigning stars and incoming international standouts. One of the players in that latter group you should know is Teruaki Sato, the NPB Triple Crown winner. Our Mike Axisa has the scouting report on the third baseman.

Closing out the rankings is a tier of left-handed pitchers who should fill out the back end of whichever rotation they land in.

Week 9 delivers another light slate with only two ranked matchups and no top 10 showdowns. That doesn't mean this week is a complete nothingburger, though. Every game for College Football Playoff hopefuls from this point forward is meaningful, and if last week taught us anything, it is that a lack of top 25 battles is the recipe for a number of upsets.

It's also that time of year when conference title races heat up. This far out from championship weekend, there are more scenarios than the mind can comprehend. But the permutations will decrease with each week, and some teams are bound to fall out of the hunt on Saturday.

One team that might not need to worry about losing to an unranked foe is No. 11 Texas. Tom Fornelli's Lock of the Week shows how the Longhorns might not need many points to defeat Mississippi State.

Here are our picks for every key matchup:

It's hard to say that Lamar Jackson and Josh Allen can ever truly upset one another, because they are arguably the two best quarterbacks in football, and their teams are always generally very good. But one side is a three-point favorite over the other in their Week 8 meeting, so if the Ravens go on the road and take down the Bills, it would qualify as an upset. And guess what? A bevy of our NFL experts think it will happen.

Tyler Sullivan would not be surprised if Jackson shows no rust in his return. The two-time MVP is expected to be in the lineup for the first time in a month after he missed three games with an ankle sprain, and if he is fully healthy, he could return to the same career-best form he showed early in the season. In their head-to-head picks column, both Jordan Dajani and Jared Dubin projected the Ravens to not only cover the spread but also win outright.

The Bills are not the only team on upset alert.

#2641. Nagelsmann still being considered for Man United job as Fenerbahçe and Juventus rumours dismissed

With Michael Carrick under considerable pressure as Manchester United manager, former Bayern Munich and Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann has been touted as a candidate to replace him for some time.

According to Sky Germany, the 39-year-old German coach is still being considered as an option to step in for Carrick should the former England international lose his job at Old Trafford.

Both Fenerbahçe and Juventus have also been linked with Nagelsmann, but the German broadcaster reports that there is no truth to either of those rumours.

The 39-year-old has been out of work since leaving his position as Germany coach following a disappointing round of 32 exit at the World Cup.

#2639. Ja Morant injury: Trail Blazers star expected to miss at least four weeks with hamstring strain

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Portland Trail Blazers star Ja Morant will miss at least the next four weeks after suffering a Grade 2 left hamstring sprain on Thursday against the Memphis Grizzlies, the team announced. Morant was facing his former team for the first time since being traded earlier this summer and exited with 7:46 remaining in the game and didn't return.

Morant missed a floater in the lane and went to grab his own miss when he appeared to suffer the injury. Morant stayed in the game for two more defensive possessions before checking out at the next stoppage of play. In 23 minutes of action, Morant finished with 14 points, three assists and two rebounds.

The 124-103 loss to the Grizzlies marked Portland's first defeat of the 2026-27 campaign after starting the season with wins over the Lakers, Kings and Suns.

Morant played in just 79 total games over the last three seasons before being traded to Portland this offseason, including logging just 20 appearances during the 2025-26 season. In his first four games with Portland, Morant was averaging 15.8 points, 5.5 assists and 2.5 rebounds.

With Morant set to miss at least the next four weeks, the Blazers will likely start veteran guard Jrue Holiday in his absence. Heading into the season, one of the main storylines and lineup questions in the NBA was who Portland would start in the backcourt.

The Trail Blazers entered the season with a self-made logjam at the position with Morant, Damian Lillard, Holiday, and former No. 3 overall pick Scoot Henderson — who is set to be a restricted free agent this summer — all on the roster. The rotation questions didn't even factor in Shaedon Shapre, who is out for the foreseeable future after suffering a torn lateral meniscus in his right knee in late August.

First-year coach Micah Nori has played Lillard the most (29.5 minutes per game) of the bunch, with Morant (25.8), Holiday (25.3) and Henderson (18.8) not far behind. With Morant out, Henderson could slide into a larger role as the first guard off the bench, even though Sidy Cissoko (22.8) is averaging more minutes per game than Henderson.

Portland ranks No. 2 in the NBA (101.3) in defensive rating through the first week and a half of the season. That number should improve even more with Holiday set to enter the starting lineup.

An unfortunate trend through the first week and a half of the season has been injuries. Morant is the latest NBA star who is set to miss time.

Current NBA stars set to miss the next few games, at minimum — with some set to be out for even longer stretches: Anthony Edwards, Paolo Banchero, Kawhi Leonard, Jaren Jackson Jr., Chet Holmgren and Jalen Williams. On top of those injuries, Brandon Ingram, Jimmy Butler, Kon Knueppel and Kristaps Porziņģis are among the players who have yet to make their season debut.

Ben Simmons, who was expected to play a significant role for the Kings this season, tore his Achilles in practice days before the season opener and will miss the entire 2026-27 season.

#2638. Ranking the top 50 MLB free agents for the 2026-27 offseason, plus landing spots for every player

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The World Series is complete, the Milwaukee Brewers are first-time champions and MLB's offseason is already underway. It won't be long until the hot stove sizzles.

To get the winter started, CBS Sports has ranked the top 50 MLB free agents for the 2026-27 offseason. These rankings are compiled through statistical and video analysis, past market research, plus vibes and general hunches. We have included players expected to make the leap from Japan's NPB and South Korea's KBO to the big leagues, but not non-tender candidates or unexpected option decisions.

Of course, this is no normal offseason. With the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1, a lockout is all but certain. How long will it last? What will baseball -- and for our purposes, contracts -- look like on the other side? Will teams and players rush to make deals before the work stoppage or delay everything until it's over? Who knows. These are the ultimate questions of the winter, and how they get answered is up to the owners and the players' union.

The two most important things to know about these rankings: First, free agency is forward-looking. What you've done in the past counts for only so much. More than ever before, teams pay players based on what they expect them to do in the future, not what they've done in their career to date. These rankings are intended to reflect that.

And second, the least important part of this exercise is the potential landing spots listed for each player. There are more than three suitors for almost every player, and it's not intended as a snub if your team isn't listed here. Here now are our top 50 free agents.

Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019. He showed few long-lasting effects from the NanoScope elbow surgery in May and remains a capital-A Ace with terrific surface stats and under-the-hood performance indicators. Skubal brings four swing-and-miss pitches to the table (four-seamer, changeup, slider, curveball), a near MLB-best ability to limit exit velocity, and elite strike-throwing ability (MLB's third-lowest walk rate since 2023). Build an ace starter in a lab and he would look a lot like Skubal. He'll play the entire 2027 season at age 30, and given the things teams can do with pitchers these days, Skubal figures to remain a frontline starter for most of a long-term contract. He's the only true balance-of-power player available in free agency this offseason. Skubal can swing a division race and a postseason series all by himself.

Morejon won't turn 28 until late February and is one of the youngest free agents available. He has been one of the game's best relievers the last three years, one who can miss bats and limit hard-hit ability at near MLB-best levels, plus you need not shelter him against right-handed batters. Morejon is a bona fide late-inning reliever who happens to throw left-handed. As good as he is out of the bullpen, it seems likely an enterprising team will give him a chance to start in 2027, and Morejon doesn't just have a chance to make it work. He has a chance to be an excellent starter thanks to his premium four-pitch mix (four-seamer, sinker, slider, changeup) and the fact he sits right at 100 mph. Morejon can give some velocity back while working longer outings and still have plenty in the tank to miss bats in the strike zone. And if starting doesn't work, he can go right back to dominating as a reliever. This ranking reflects my belief in Morejon as a starter. There is one potential red flag: Morejon was not available in Games 2-4 of the NLDS with what Padres manager Craig Stammen called "stickiness" in his shoulder. Interested teams will no doubt closely scrutinize Morejon's medicals.

Rogers was never able to fully work off the early season stinkers that inflated his ERA, though this is free agency, and ERA is close to the last thing on the minds of interested teams. You're looking forward in free agency, not backward. The underlying performance indicators are very strong, specifically the ability to get chase and avoid the barrel with four pitches (four-seamer, sinker, changeup, sweeper) that light up analytical models. Rogers also has a fifth-pitch cutter and has shown the ability to hammer the strike zone the last two years. There are some lefty Zack Wheeler vibes here. When Wheeler became a free agent after 2019, he already had the analytical stamp of approval, and the belief was he could get to another level with fine-tuning and good health. That is exactly what happened. Lefty Wheeler would obviously be the best-case scenario outcome for Rogers, but the bottom line is he will play the entire 2027 season at age 29, and he throws strikes with four pitches that the pitch data models already consider above average. More than a few teams will undoubtedly see Rogers as a pitcher who is a tweak or two away from finding another gear.

The Hanshin Tigers will post Sato for MLB teams this offseason, the NPB club announced in late October. He will play the entire 2027 season at age 28 and is coming off a .306/.383/.609 slash line with 39 home runs, which won him Japan's first Triple Crown since Munetaka Murakami in 2022. Sato has a similar skill set but is not quite Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll.

It has been a roller coaster year for Peralta, who flopped with the Mets, rebounded with the Rays, then faced the Brewers (his former team) in the World Series and lost. The post-deadline stint with Tampa salvaged Peralta's free agent year. They made several adjustments, most notably raising his arm angle and getting him to pitch exclusively from the stretch, and the result was a livelier fastball and also better command. He's still five-and-fly Freddy. Even the best version of Peralta won't pitch deep into games and can be a tough watch because he nibbles and throws so many pitches per inning. They tend to be good innings, though, and the guy never misses a start. Worst case, Peralta is a mid-rotation starter you can count on to take the ball every fifth day. The best case is someone who can front a contender's rotation. Fastball Freddy was always going to be a great bounceback candidate this offseason. The Rays just beat everyone to it at the trade deadline.

In what was his worst season as a hitter since his rookie year in 2021, Chisholm was still a league-average bat in 2026, and his top-shelf defense and baserunning still landed him at 3.5 WAR. Chisholm is a style-over-substance player who is not for everyone, but his second base defense and near-MLB-best baserunning skills give him a very high floor. He's a reasonable bet for 20-ish home runs with the potential to go 30-30, and Chisholm has improved his plate discipline enough to run walk rates north of 10% the last two years. The downside is his propensity to swing and miss. Chisholm has posted below-average in-zone contact rates throughout his career and contact rates that low always come with risk. That risk is mitigated somewhat by the secondary skills (defense, etc.) and the fact that Chisholm will play the entire 2027 season at age 29. You probably don't want him as your best or second-best player, but he's also an overqualified No. 6-7 hitter who brings so much else to the table.

The 32-year-old Suzuki is one of only four qualified hitters to post a 125 OPS+ or better each of the last four seasons. He's a right-handed hitter with unerring patience and strong ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) at a time when right-handed power is in shockingly short supply. Suzuki is also sneaky fast, though don't expect him to pile up big stolen base totals. Thanks to improved jumps with the help of outfield coach Quintin Berry, Suzuki made the leap from average at best defender to legitimately excellent this season. The team that signs him will likely be the team that believes his defensive improvement is sticky. Even if it isn't, Suzuki's righty thump is a scarce commodity these days, and will land him a nice contract even as he prepares to enter his mid-30s. At worst, you'll get a power-and-patience hitter who is comfortable playing in the spotlight.

King has reportedly already opted out of the final two years and $58 million remaining on his contract and he should have no trouble beating that this offseason, even if it is more total dollars over more years but at a lower annual salary. King is a five-pitch righty with an extreme east/west attack -- the movement on King's sinker, sweeper, and changeup border on cartoonish -- who makes his living by limiting hard contact more than he does missing bats and blowing hitters away. He has consistently outperformed the various ERA estimators (FIP, xERA, etc.) throughout his career, and when you do it over hundreds of innings, it's a skill, not a fluke. King will turn 32 in May and his fastball is getting hit a little harder with each passing year. There is some blow-up potential here. Still, King is a high-end No. 2 starter and he's regarded as a Grade-A clubhouse guy, which is not nothing. He's instantly become a fan favorite wherever he's played.

Always a strong hitter, Arozarena had a career-best season in 2026, during which he hit offspeed pitches (changeups, splitters, etc.) better than ever. His superpower has always been his ability to punish fastballs and breaking balls at above-average rates. Now he added the "hit soft stuff" club to his bag. Arozarena will play the entire 2027 season at age 32 and he offers righty thump at a time when it's very hard to find, plus he's shown time and time again that he is unafraid of big moments. He'll also chip in 20-plus steals despite a lack of blazing speed. The downside is Arozarena is basically a DH at this point in his career. Poor jumps, poor routes, poor range, poor arm. He's a liability in the outfield and whichever team signs him would be wise to DH him exclusively.

Over the last four seasons, Jeffers has reduced his strikeout rate from 27.8% to 20.2% to 19.6% to an excellent 17.9% in 2026. He opened his stance a little and moved further back in the box a few years ago, felt good about it, and has continued to open and widen his stance a tiny bit more with each passing year. Jeffers offers right-handed pull power and strong plate discipline to go with his continually improving contact skills. The downside is his defense behind the plate, which grades out poorly every which way. Blocking, throwing, framing, etc. The offensive bar at catcher is on the floor. Jeffers clears it with plenty of room to spare, enough that teams will overlook the shaky glovework. He will turn 30 in June and is the best catcher to hit free agency since Willson Contreras in 2022.

Arraez continues to hum along, posting Dead Ball Era contact rates while making fans of every team wish they had him. Offensively, he's the same player he's always been. Arraez is the game's best bat-to-ball guy. He'll contend for a batting title, hit single-digit home runs, and rarely walk because he so easily puts the ball in play. How much do you buy into his improvement in the field? Arraez might have been the single worst defensive player in baseball prior to 2026, then he worked with infield guru Ron Washington with the Giants and became a legitimately above-average defender at second base. Above average according to both the eye test and the numbers, which isn't always the case with defense. If you think that defensive improvement is real, you see a 4-WAR player who will turn only 30 soon after Opening Day. If you don't, you see a one-tool player who barely scraped 1 WAR in 2024 and 2025. Don't be surprised if Arraez again has trouble drumming up interest as a free agent.

Rake Bauers (finally) lived up to the nickname this year and carried it over into the postseason, particularly during the NLCS. Long an exit velocity and hard-hit rate darling, Bauers fully tapped into his power in 2026 thanks to a more open stance and moving back in the box and further off the plate. That allowed him to see the ball better and get his bat into the hitting position on time more consistently. I'm not 100% sold on those adjustments solving his career-long issues with lefties, though at least there is a tangible reason to believe in his great left-on-left performance this season. Bauers can be an adventure in the field (he has played outfield in the past) and he just turned 31. A few teams will look for the next Jake Bauers rather than pay the actual Jake Bauers.

There is no doubting Lowe's power. He's hit well over 30 homers per 600 plate appearances throughout his career. There simply aren't many middle infielders who hit the ball over the fence that consistently, and those who can are infrequently available. Prior to 2026, Lowe was close to a one-tool player, but he made huge gains in the field thanks to Pittsburgh's coaching staff. How huge? Lowe went from -14 outs above average in 2025 to +15 in 2026. It's the largest year-over-year improvement in Statcast history. The power has always been real and the defensive improvement is encouraging. The downsides are near-bottom-of-the-league contact rates, a declining walk rate, a lengthy injury history, and the fact that Lowe is already 32. That all adds up to an uncomfortable amount of collapse risk.

Gray has reportedly mulled retirement over the last few offseasons, but he intends to pitch in 2027. He's as crafty as ever, using six pitches regularly and giving hitters every look. Hard, soft, sharp break, big movement, etc. Gray's stuff works in such a way that he seems to get a quick first or second pitch out every inning, allowing him to pitch deep into games. He completed six innings 22 times in his 29 starts this past season, which makes him a workhorse by 2026 standards. Gray will pitch the entire 2027 season at age 37 and he's lost enough velocity to shrink his margin of error meaningfully, which creates some over-the-cliff risk. Still, the 14-year veteran is not out of place as the No. 2 starter in a postseason rotation.

Being boring is an underrated closer trait and Bednar, 32, has it. He won't beat himself with walks, he limits hard contact, he misses bats, he's effective against righties and lefties, and he proved he's built for the postseason and big markets during his time in New York. His low-90s splitter is an equalizer that seems impossible to square up. Furthermore, Bednar is a low-maintenance pitcher who's shown a willingness to go multiple innings and work as a setup man. He won't make a stink about his role. There has been some age-related velocity loss and he had to abandon his curveball at times this past season because he had so much trouble commanding it. Otherwise, Bednar is a plug-and-play high-leverage reliever.

Every contender could use a player like Dubón. He's a true super utility guy who can play every position except catcher -- and play it well. Offensively, Dubón is an aggressive bat-to-ball player with a knack for ideal launch angles, which, in English, means he's a line drive hitter. He obliterated his previous career high in games played and plate appearances this past season and handled the workload well. Dubón is older than you may realize (he turns 33 in July), but he's been valuable everywhere he's played, and he's the kind of player every manager loves. The ability to play everywhere, put the ball in play, and be relentlessly upbeat is the ideal modern utility man.

Offensively, Happ has "old player skills." He has always walked a lot, which keeps his on-base percentage respectable even as his batting average has taken a hit. You can also pencil him in for 20-25 homers. Dingers and discipline typically age well. Defensively, Happ remains Gold Glove-caliber thanks to a great first step and a strong arm. He won't wow you with highlight reel catches, but he will catch everything he's supposed to catch and then some. Happ will play most of next season at age 32 and there has been enough slippage in his contact rates and exit velocity that I'm comfortable calling them worrisome. Age-related decline might be right around the corner, though the skill set suggests a gentle decline rather than a complete collapse. I have more faith in Happ being a steady contributor over the next one or two years than some position players ranked above him. There's just less upside.

It is incorrect to say Iglesias was as good as ever in 2026. He was terrific, to be sure, but the contact allowed is getting louder and he's lost two ticks off his fastball the last two years. That is a normal baseball thing for someone who has a big career workload (for a reliever) and will pitch all of next season at age 37. Iglesias has closer chops and his changeup is one of the very best pitches in the sport, and all you need as a one-inning reliever is that one great pitch. At this age, there's always a chance it all comes crashing down. Iglesias will -- and should -- continue to get well-paying one-year contracts until that happens.

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Seibu announced on Oct. 30 that Taira will be posted this offseason.

Long a pitch data darling, Mahle had the best stretch of his career after joining the Braves at the trade deadline. They ramped up his splitter usage and tweaked his slider a tad, and also got him to live in the shadows of the strike zone more often. Mahle will not continue posting a 1.99 ERA. No one is that good. He has always passed the analytical test, though, and he's finally healthy after arm injuries limited him to 125 innings from 2023-25. Health will always be a question. That's just the way it is with pitchers who've gotten hurt repeatedly. Mahle just turned 32, though, and we finally saw proof of concept this year. This deep into the free agent rankings, every pitcher carries some kind of risk. I like Mahle's upside more than the rest.

A bad luck broken leg (he was hit by a comebacker) derailed Holmes in 2026. He got hurt in May, was traded while on the injured list, then returned in August without his usual velocity. Even while working in the low 90s rather than mid-90s, Holmes remained one of the game's very best ground ball artists. His sweeper and cutter are above-average weapons according to the pitch data models, and Holmes picked up a nice kick-change with the Mets. It's not everything, but teams will like that Holmes is postseason and big-market battle-tested following his time with the two New York teams, and that he has experience as a starter and a reliever. The ground balls give Holmes a reasonably high floor. He's very likely to be useful in some capacity in 2027, and it helps that he's regarded as coachable and a strong teammate. The declining velocity, declining strikeout rate, and the fact that Holmes will pitch all of next season at age 34 will chill his market a bit.

Velocity is important for every pitcher and that is especially true for Gausman. He's made a living throwing fastballs almost literally down the middle to set up his all-world splitter. Hitters chase the splitter because they think it's a fastball and take the fastball for strikes because they sit on the splitter. When Gausman sat 95-96 mph at his peak, he dominated. Now that he's closer to 93-94 mph most nights, it doesn't work quite as well. He toyed with a sweeper late in the season and I would expect the team that signs him to hone in on that pitch (or some other breaking ball) to mitigate the velocity loss. Gausman will pitch the entire 2027 season at age 36 and he's as good a bet to make 32 starts next year as any pitcher in the game, which is not nothing.

France has reinvented himself a few times over the years and the current version is the best version yet. He opened his stance a bit this season and the result was much more hard contact, specifically against fastballs. France has always posted solid contact and walk rates. Now, he's getting his bat through the zone a little quicker and producing more on contact. Also, France has made himself into an excellent defensive first baseman. One of the very best in the game, in fact. His track record as a top hitter is one year, basically, and France will turn 33 next summer. The dearth of quality right-handed bats could still land him a multi-year contract.

You can talk yourself into Mize, 30 in May, having untapped upside as a former No. 1 overall draft pick who pitched pretty well this past season around a series of groin injuries before being traded to San Diego at the deadline. You can also talk yourself into Mize being fool's gold because he doesn't have a plus pitch, frequents the injured list, and hasn't impressed despite pitching in pitcher-friendly ballparks his entire career. The things teams can do with pitchers these days are amazing, really. I would never rule out a prime-aged pitcher figuring things out and carving out a strong second phase to his career. Eventually, though, the shine of the "former No. 1 overall pick" thing wears off.

May turned only 29 in September and he's topped 130 innings in back-to-back years after throwing 101 innings total around injuries, including UCL surgery, from 2021-24. Even after the injuries, May still lives in the mid-to-upper-90s with his sinker, and pitch data models are fond of his sweeper and curveball. It is not the best sign, though, that the Brewers, who know pitching as well as any team, couldn't fully unlock May after making him their big deadline rotation addition. Still, the combination of age and high-octane stuff makes him a nice upside play on a short-term contract, particularly for a rebuilding team that is willing to run him out there every fifth day regardless of results.

A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon Ham Fighters are expected to post Itoh, who turned 29 in August, this winter.

The only question is health. Soroka's 116 innings this season were his most since his National League Rookie of the Year runner-up season in 2019. Back then, Soroka was a sinker specialist and ground ball machine. These days, he's a low-to-mid-90s four-seam fastball guy with a slurvy breaking ball that falls somewhere between a curveball and a slider. Soroka also has a cutter, a changeup, and, yep, still the sinker. The breaking ball grades out as his best pitch, though everything plays up because he tunnels well and is a good strike-thrower. I like Soroka, who will pitch most of next season at 29, more as a reliever, possibly even as a multi-inning high-leverage guy. The skill set is that of a back-end starter though, and you needn't squint too much to see upside beyond that.

The Nationals did terrific work signing Griffin to a low-cost one-year contract ($5.5 million) last offseason. He had an All-Star first half, then Washington flipped him for four prospects at the trade deadline. Griffin added about three pitches during his three years with the Yomiuri Giants in Japan and now is one of baseball's few true seven-pitch pitchers. He's an extreme strike-thrower and Griffin tunnels his pitches in such a way that his entire arsenal punches above its weight. There isn't one or two individual pitches that stand out, but they all work together well. Griffin will turn 32 in July and he's built for a full season's workload. He may not have the upside you can dream on like a few pitchers ranked ahead of him, but Griffin feels like a decent bet to be a top 75-ish starter in 2027 as long as he stays healthy.

Martinez, 36, posted the lowest strikeout rate among qualified pitchers in 2026, and also the 14th-lowest ERA. He's traded whiffs for weak contact the last few years and, frankly, I don't think you can reasonably expect him to post baseball's fourth-lowest ground ball rate and sixth-lowest home run rate again next season. Those are two things that rarely go together, even with Martinez's propensity for weak contact. His high arm angle creates an unusual look for hitters and creates tremendous downward action on his sinker and changeup. Martinez also has a cutter and a curveball. He made 31 starts and threw 180 innings for the Rays this year, so he can be a regular member of the rotation, if needed. Moving forward, Martinez might be most valuable as the high-end swingman he was from 2022-25.

There are days when Imanaga looks like an ace and days when he simply can't keep the ball in the park. He's an extreme fly ball pitcher who has averaged one homer every 4 ⅔ innings or so the last two years. Imanaga regained the tick of velocity he lost in 2025, but we're still talking about a pitcher who lives in the 91-93 mph range most days. It's an upshoot fastball, meaning it gets a lot of empty swings at the top of the zone thanks to his arm angle and release height, but when Imanaga misses his spot, he pays a big price. His splitter and sweeper are good enough secondary pitches. Imanaga will pitch most of next season at age 33 and he's a pitching nerd who is willing to tinker, which perhaps gives him a chance to reshape his arsenal as he gets into his mid-30s.

31. LHP JoJo Romero32. RHP Jonathan Loáisiga 33. RHP Paul Blackburn 34. RHP Evan Phillips 35. LHP Alex Vesia

An appendectomy split Romero's season in two. He was great during the Brewers' postseason run and has been one of the game's better lefty relievers for four years now. His sinker/sweeper attack is plenty good enough that Romero does not have to be sheltered against righties. Loáisiga had his first healthy season in four years and got back to throwing upper-90s bowling ball sinkers. He won't miss many bats at this point in his career, but he will generate a ton of weak contact on the ground. A good defensive infield is a must behind him. Blackburn thrived in his first season as a full-time reliever and, like Loáisiga, he did it with a weak ground ball contact rate rather than strikeouts. He pitches like a starter in relief in that he uses five pitches regularly, and held up across multi-inning outings all season. Phillips ran into some home run trouble when he first returned from Tommy John surgery in July, but otherwise continued to rack up whiffs with his fastball/sweeper combo. Vesia's fastball is mostly 90-91 mph these days and he walks too many batters, but he is fearless, and he can still get his heater by hitters at the top rail thanks to the movement traits.

36. 2B Gleyber Torres 37. C Carson Kelly38. 1B/3B Alec Bohm 39. UTIL Edmundo Sosa40. OF Michael Conforto   41. DH George Springer

These days, Torres is a contact/walks guy who might hit 15 homers and provide what can charitably be described as below-average defense and baserunning. He is not out of place as a contender's leadoff hitter given his on-base ability, though it's name value more than one-field value at this point. Kelly may be ranked too low here given his last two seasons and the general lack of quality catchers in free agency. He's an above-average contact/plate discipline guy with limited hard-hit ability and an unfortunate knack for ground ball contact. Defensively, Kelly moves well below the plate but is not much of a framer or thrower. He fits best as a platoon or half-time catcher, not as the undisputed starter. Bohm has solid contact quality data and a history of hitting lefties hard. He can play first and third bases in the sense that he can stand at first and third base, but you won't like what you see. Bohm has been miscast as a middle-of-the-order hitter and everyday third baseman over the last few years. The 30-year-old has real value as a righty platoon bat, though. Sosa had a down year at the plate despite no change under the hood (exit velocity, etc.). He has a long track record of hammering lefties, plus you can put him almost anywhere on the field. Every team could use a bench guy like that. Conforto showed very promising underlying data during his miserable 2025 and turned it into results in 2026. He's a nifty lefty platoon guy at this point in his career. Springer's resurgence in 2025 did not carry over into 2026. He'll play all of next season at age 37 and there isn't much juice left in his bat. The sport's lack of quality right-handed bats could get him a job with a contender, though he needs to DH regularly to stay healthy and productive.

42. CF Daulton Varsho 43. RHP Nick Pivetta 44. RHP Shane Bieber 45. LHP Kris Bubic 46. C Tyler Stephenson

September wrist surgery bumps Varsho down these rankings even though he's the best defensive center fielder in free agency. The ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) is below average and he is not a disciplined hitter. You can dream on Varsho returning to his 2025 form, but, with his 31st birthday coming up next year, the more likely outcome is a glove-first player who fights to a draw as a league-average hitter and posts an on-base percentage that starts with a 2. Pivetta missed most of this season with a flexor injury and that triggered a clause that gives the Padres the option to walk away from the two years and $32 remaining on his contract. I'm not 100% convinced it will happen, but it is possible. Pivetta will turn 34 in February and will need his stuff to play better than it did after the injury to make postseason starts in 2027. Injuries, including Tommy John surgery, have limited Bieber to 108 innings over the last three years, and he made only 11 wobbly starts in 2026. He will turn 32 in May and his command is so exceptional that he can survive with the low-90s velocity he showed this summer, but it is a tightrope walk these days. Bubic has an outlier fastball thanks to its rise and his unusual release point. Giving him a chance to start for the last two years was a worthwhile experiment, though the persistent arm injuries likely mean it's time to put a pin in that and turn him back into a full-time reliever. Stephenson has all-fields power and checks analytical boxes with his hard-hit data. He is in the conversation for the worst defensive catcher in the sport, though. A team with a good catching development program might convince themselves they can coach him up to average defense.

47. LHP Matthew Boyd 48. LHP David Peterson 49. LHP Robbie Ray50. LHP Patrick Sandoval

Boyd will pitch all of next season at 36 and his package of secondary pitches is unique given the movement and his arm angle. He is fearless and could maybe benefit from throwing fewer strikes. Boyd has the stuff to get chases, and his mistakes in the zone tend to leave the yard. The Cubs got Peterson's career back on the rails following a June trade. Much of that was pitch sequencing and playing in front of the best defense in baseball. The 31-year-old's upside is a No. 4-5 starter you can pencil in for 20-something starts. Ray's season went downhill after his trade to San Diego. His stuff is down several ticks from his prime and his strikeout rate has cratered now that he's in his mid-30s. If you need someone to throw 110 pitches to get 13-15 outs every fifth day, he's your guy. Sandoval did not have the smoothest return from Tommy John surgery this season, though I am curious to see what he looks like as he gets further away from surgery. He showed some good secondary pitch shapes and an ability to keep the ball on the ground. I reckon he'll outperform at least a few of the pitchers we have ranked ahead of him in 2027.
