#2637. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2634. MLB qualifying offer: Predicting who will get a QO this offseason, plus how the $23.15 million contract works

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Brewers have been crowned the 2026 World Series champions and the 2026-27 offseason is already underway. More than 100 players became free agents the day after the World Series ended, and soon teams will have to make decisions about contract options and qualifying offers.

The qualifying offer (QO) entitles teams to draft-pick compensation in the event that they lose a free agent to another team. The QO is a one-year deal set at the average of the top 125 salaries in baseball. This offseason, it's worth a record $23.15 million, according to the New York Post. That is up from $22.025 million last year, $21.05 million the year before, and $20.325 million the year before that.

Teams have until five days after the end of the World Series to tender their free agents the QO, and players who receive it then have until 4 p.m. ET on Nov. 17 to accept or reject. Players who accept the QO remain with their team and cannot be traded without their consent until June 15. Players who reject the QO become free agents with draft-pick compensation attached.

Simple, right? The process is, but the decisions aren't always. With that in mind, let's run down this offseason's QO candidates, as well as explain the draft-pick compensation rules.

Yes, the QO is still a thing this offseason. The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and the next CBA could change the QO rules, maybe even eliminate it entirely. That said, until that happens, the QO remains in place. Decisions to tender the QO (made by the team) and decisions to accept or reject the QO (made by the player) are due before the CBA expires.

Once upon a time, teams that lost an eligible free agent received a compensation draft pick after the first round. It was nice and easy. The current rules are a bit more complicated. Here are compensation rules for teams that lose a qualified free agent:

Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round)

Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round)

The Athletics, Brewers, Cardinals, Diamondbacks, Guardians, Mariners, Marlins, Orioles, Pirates, Rays, Reds, Rockies, Royals, Tigers, and Twins received revenue sharing this season, so the first two scenarios apply to them. The Blue Jays, Braves, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, Red Sox, and Yankees will pay competitive balance tax (CBT), so they're in the third scenario. The Angels, Astros, Giants, Nationals, Rangers, and White Sox neither received revenue sharing nor paid CBT. They're in the fourth bucket.

Now here are the penalties for signing a qualified free agent:

The Blue Jays, Braves, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, Red Sox, and Yankees will pay CBT and are in the first group. The Athletics, Brewers, Cardinals, Diamondbacks, Guardians, Mariners, Marlins, Orioles, Pirates, Rays, Reds, Rockies, Royals, Tigers, and Twins received revenue sharing and are in the second group. The Angels, Astros, Giants, Nationals, Rangers, and White Sox are the third group. Got it? Good.

Thirteen players received the QO last offseason: Trent Grisham, Shota Imanaga, Gleyber Torres, and Brandon Woodruff accepted the QO; Zac Gallen, Michael King, and Kyle Schwarber declined but signed new contracts to remain with their teams; Bo Bichette, Dylan Cease, Edwin Díaz, Kyle Tucker, Ranger Suárez, and Framber Valdez rejected the QO and signed with new teams, giving their former clubs compensatory draft picks. Teams do not gain or lose draft picks for re-signing their own qualified free agent.

Players are eligible for the QO as long as they spent the entire 2026 season with one team and did not receive the QO previously. That means several high-profile free agents are not eligible for the QO this offseason. Here are the notables:

CHANGED TEAMS Luis Arraez Kevin Gausman (also received QO previously) Casey Mize Freddy Peralta Tarik Skubal Daulton Varsho

PREVIOUSLY RECEIVED QO Bo Bichette (opt out) Sonny Gray (mutual option) Michael King (opt out)  Nick Martinez

The Tigers traded Skubal, the reigning two-time AL Cy Young winner, to the Dodgers for a three-prospect package at the deadline. MLB Pipeline currently ranks those players as Detroit's No. 1 (Zyhir Hope), No. 3 (River Ryan), and No. 9 (Brady Smith) prospects. That's a much better haul than the compensation draft pick the Tigers would have received had they kept Skubal all year and made him the QO. Anyway, these free agents are among those not eligible for the QO this offseason.

This is not the best free agent class and, as a result, I count only two stone-cold locks to receive a QO: Randy Arozarena (Mariners) and Seiya Suzuki (Cubs). The Mariners and Cubs would be thrilled if Arozarena and Seiya accepted the QO and returned next season on one-year contracts that aren't too much of a raise. Arozarena made $15.65 million this year. Suzuki earned $18 million. The jump to $23.15 million isn't big enough to shy away from the QO, plus these are really good players. Arozarena and Suzuki will receive the QO and decline it.

Although Arozarena and Suzuki are the only locks to get the QO, in my opinion, there are three other free agents-to-be who seem like pretty good bets to receive it. Here are those three players:

Ryan Jeffers, Twins: Jeffers will be the best catcher to hit the open market since Willson Contreras four years ago. He missed time with a hamate injury this year and his defense isn't great, plus he'll turn 30 next June. Those seem like nitpicks compared to the offense he brings to the table at the catcher position. The only reason I don't think Jeffers is a lock to get the QO is the fact that the Twins have shaved roughly $50 million off their payroll the last four years. They might get thrifty.

Brandon Lowe, Pirates: Pittsburgh knocked it out of the park with the Mike Burrows-for-Lowe-and-Mason Montgomery three-team trade with the Astros and Rays. Montgomery is a bullpen ace and Lowe slugged 35 home runs, the most by a Pirate since Josh Bell hit 37 in 2019. Lowe's age (32), poor contact rates, and history of poor defense (though not in 2026) create collapse risk. Also, the Pirates run a bottom 10 payroll every season. I expect Lowe to get the QO. I just wouldn't be surprised if the Pirates decide not to risk him taking it, thereby soaking up 20% or so of their 2027 payroll.

Trevor Rogers, Orioles: Rogers, 29 in November, was a bright spot in an otherwise lost season for the O's. He stayed healthy and threw a career-high 169 ⅔ innings, and pitched exceptionally well after June 1: 2.90 ERA with under-the-hood numbers to match (2.89 FIP and 3.10 expected ERA). Rogers might be the second-best free agent starter behind Skubal given his success the last two years and (more importantly) analytically friendly arsenal. During the president of baseball operations Mike Elias era, the Orioles haven't always done the most sensible thing when it comes to spending money. I think it's 99% certain the O's will give Rogers the QO, but 99% is not 100%.

My hunch is teams will be conservative with their QO decisions this offseason because a new CBA is coming, and no one knows what the game's economic landscape will look like next year. Will there be a salary cap? More punitive CBT penalties? I would expect teams to err on the side of caution when it comes to potentially committing $23.15 million to one player. Even a good player they may want back, but not necessarily at $23.15 million in 2027. Here are three borderline QO cases:

David Bednar, Yankees: Bednar has proven he can close games in New York, which is not nothing, but he did just turn 32, and the $23.15 million QO would make him the highest-paid reliever in baseball. I think the Yankees want to bring Bednar back next season. Enough to risk him accepting the QO? When the potential reward is a dinky draft pick after the fourth round given their CBT status? That I'm not sold on. A multi-year contract at a lower annual salary is the much more likely path to Bednar returning to the Yankees.

Jazz Chisholm Jr., Yankees: Even in a down year, Chisholm was a 3.5-WAR player thanks to the breadth of his skill set. He hit 19 homers, he stole 41 bases, and he was fourth among second basemen with +13 outs above average. The all-around game and the fact that Chisholm will play the entire 2027 season at age 29 would seem to make him a slam dunk QO candidate. My sense is the Yankees won't commit any significant payroll to next season without first seeing what the new CBA brings, which is exactly what they did before the last lockout. I think the Yankees value the payroll flexibility (i.e. the certainty that Chisholm won't take the QO) more than the post-fourth round compensation pick they would receive if he signed elsewhere.

Adrian Morejon, Padres: Morejon will be an interesting test case for San Diego's new ownership. He is outstanding, one of the five or six best relievers in baseball, and he'll play the entire 2027 season at age 28. The QO would make Morejon the highest-paid reliever in the game, but only if he takes it, and his age and effectiveness would seem to make that unlikely. Do the Padres roll the dice and give Morejon the QO, and risk sinking $23.15 million into a (great) setup man, or not bother because they're only in line to receive a draft pick after the fourth round if he leaves? Díaz, Josh Hader (from the Padres), and Raisel Iglesias are the only relievers to get the QO in the last seven years. Is Morejon in that class?

The Baltimore Ravens are dealing with a nightmare situation at quarterback. The team is playing on Thursday night this week, and with just barely 48 hours to go until kickoff, the Ravens still have no idea who their starting quarterback will be against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

One possible option could be Kedon Slovis, who was added to Baltimore's roster on Tuesday after being signed off the Packers' practice squad, according to the Ringer. This signing should give you an idea of just how desperate the Ravens are at the quarterback position this week: Slovis has never started a game in his NFL career, but he might be forced to start this week. If that happens, he'll be taking the field with only two practices under his belt in Baltimore.

The Ravens likely wanted to bring in someone familiar with the coaching staff, which would explain their decision to add Slovis. Ravens' QB coach Israel Woolfork held the same job in Arizona last season during a year where Slovis was on the roster, so the two are familiar with each other.

The 2024 undrafted rookie has only thrown two passes in his career and both of those were while he was working mop-up duty for the Cardinals last season.

The Ravens also brought in 2024 UFL MVP Adrian Martinez for a workout, according to The Athletic. The 26-year-old has had stints with both the 49ers and Jets in his career, but he's only played in one game ever and that came last season for San Francisco. As of right now, Martinez hasn't been signed.

If you're wondering how the Ravens got to a point where they might have to start a player who's only thrown two career passes, it's because their quarterback room took a beating on Sunday in Baltimore's 36-10 loss to Buffalo.

Lamar Jackson is headed for injured reserve after suffering a thumb injury on Baltimore's first offensive play of the game. His backup, Tyler Huntley, is also out after injuring his toe against Buffalo. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano played the majority of the game for the Ravens on Sunday, but he's dealing with an ankle injury and Ravens' coach Jesse Minter isn't sure what his availability is going to be with Baltimore playing on a short week.

"To Joe's credit, he's kind of fighting through a couple things he's dealing with, but expect him to have a chance to play on Thursday," Minter said after the team's Monday walkthrough practice.

If Fagnano is healthy enough to play, then he'll be the starter. The undrafted rookie out of UConn impressed the coaching staff in training camp and ended up winning a spot on the roster. After being forced into action against the Bills, he went just 10-of-21 for 91 yards with an interception, but that was after a week where he took zero first-team snaps (Third-string quarterbacks never get any first-team reps during the season). If Fagnano starts this week, Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle will create a game plan more tailored to his rookie QB.

If Fagnano can't go, Baltimore will roll with either Slovis or Austin Reed. The Ravens signed Reed to their practice squad on Monday and he's somewhat familiar with the offense because he spent part of training camp and the preseason in Baltimore before being released in late August. Reed played in all three of Baltimore's preseason games this year and he ended up finishing 6 of 12 for 59 yards with one touchdown and one interception along with one touchdown run.

Reed, who entered the NFL as an undrafted rookie in 2024, has never thrown a pass in a regular-season game.

On Slovis' end, since he was signed off another team's practice squad, that means he has a guaranteed spot on the Ravens' 53-man roster this week. If Fagnano plays, it wouldn't be surprising if the Ravens have three active quarterbacks this week as insurance for the rookie's injured ankle.

Right now, the Ravens only have three options at quarterback this week and they're all players who went undrafted. There was some speculation that the Ravens might try to add Tyson Bagent in a trade, but with the Bears playing on Monday night in Seattle, they likely weren't open to trading their backup QB since they needed him for the game. With the Ravens playing on Thursday night week, they needed to add someone quickly, and although they didn't get a trade done, they did end up settling on Reed and Slovis.

The Ravens could still add another quarterback before Thursday, but if they don't, they'll have to roll with Fagnano, Reed or Slovis, three guys who have appeared in three career NFL games combined.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only two days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

As expected, Mets infielder Bo Bichette has picked up his $42 million player option for 2027, reports The Athletic. He holds another $42 million player option for 2028. Still only 28, Bichette had a poor first season in Queens, posting a .702 OPS with 18 home runs while showing growing pains as he transitioned from shortstop over to third base.

For now, the Mets are set on the infield with Bichette at third, Francisco Lindor at short, and Marcus Semien at second. They must figure out first base, and it is possible they will make a trade to shake up that veteran infield. Moving Semien would be ideal, but it may not be doable. Lindor's name figures to pop up in trade rumors against this offseason.

The Diamondbacks are expected to listen to offers for second baseman Ketel Marte, reports the Arizona Republic. The D-backs entertained trade offers last offseason, but were unable to find a match. Marte has full no-trade protection and can direct where he lands, if he wants to leave Arizona at all. His desire to change teams is unknown.

Marte, 33, had a down year by his standards in 2026. He also went AWOL in August, prompting the D-backs to put him on the restricted list. Manager Torey Lovullo later revealed it was the fourth straight season Marte missed a game without permission. Beyond the on-field fit, teams will have to weigh the potential clubhouse impact and headaches.

The Seibu Lions in Japan will make right-hander Kaima Taira available to MLB teams via the posting system this offseason, the team announced Friday. The posting is expected to be made official in the coming days. Once that happens, Taira will have 45 days to negotiate and sign with an MLB team, otherwise he will return to Japan in 2027.

We ranked Taira as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason. Here's our write-up:

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man.

Taira, 27 next month, threw 146 innings with a 1.36 ERA and 141 strikeouts this past season. He actually had higher ERAs as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, though he has been excellent throughout his career in Japan, and has the bat-missing power stuff that tends to translate well to MLB. Taira figures to be highly sought after in the coming weeks.

The trading season resumed Thursday and the Red Sox were involved in the offseason's first two trades. First, they sent utility man Nate Eaton to the Athletics for minor-league righty Jareth Rayo, the team announced. The A's recently named former Red Sox assistant general manager Taylor Smith their new president of baseball operations. His first move was bringing in Eaton, a player he's presumably familiar with given their overlapping time in Boston.

Next, the Red Sox traded infielder Tsung-Che Cheng to the Tigers for cash, the team announced. Cheng, 25, is a glove-first utility man who appeared in 14 games with Boston this past season. Both the Cheng and Eaton trades open up 40-man roster spots for the Red Sox, who still must open three more spots to accommodate their seven players on the 60-day injured list. They must be activated no later than this coming Monday.

#2627. How can Thunder survive Chet Holmgren's absence? Rookie Aday Mara becomes vital as trade rumors swirl

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Oklahoma City Thunder announced that Chet Holmgren underwent treatment on Friday to address a small patellar tendon tear in his right knee, an issue that will keep him out of the lineup for the next 8-10 weeks.

With Jalen Williams out for the season following a gruesome leg injury and Cason Wallace set to miss most of the season after surgery to repair a torn labrum in his left shoulder, the Thunder are now without three of their top six players on the roster less than a month into the season.

The Thunder are off to a 4-1 start so far, but a lopsided loss to the Dallas Mavericks on Wednesday night with Holmgren out offered a glimpse into how challenging life will be with another star on the shelf.

For a team that began the season as the co-favorites in the Western Conference alongside the San Antonio Spurs with a win total over 60, now they face a challenge maintaining a spot in the top four in the West after losing so much of their expected production two weeks into the season.

Oklahoma City has been dominant in recent seasons largely due to its tremendous depth, but this summer saw them take the first steps in shedding that due to the perils of the second apron and rising costs of keeping a talented young core together. Gone are three established contributors in Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe, and while those were understandable cost-cutting measures, they exacerbate the challenge of dealing with serious injuries to key players at all three levels of the floor.

If there's a silver lining, it's that Holmgren's injury will only cost him a couple of months. But with Wallace and Williams out, losing one of the league's best rim protectors will be extremely difficult to deal with. This was already going to be a challenging season for coach Mark Daigneault without two key backcourt stars, but now he has to shuffle his lineups across the board with Holmgren out.

The Thunder probably hoped to bring their rookie big man along slowly, but with Holmgren out, the 7-foot-3 center out of Michigan will have to take on a larger spot in the rotation. Mara impressed in spot duty in his debut against Victor Wembanyama on opening night, showing why the Thunder drafted him to combat their chief rival with a rare player with the size and length to bother him -- and alleviate the stress Holmgren faces dealing with Wemby.

Mara then picked up his first double-double in a win over the Phoenix Suns on Monday, as he got his first extended burn with Holmgren out, scoring 11 points and pulling down 10 boards in 20 minutes. He was less effective in 21 minutes against the Mavs, and the Thunder will have to navigate the ups and downs of the rookie experience as Mara gets more comfortable in his expanded role.

Offensively, Mara is a play-finisher at the rim. So far this season, 80% of his field goal attempts have come within four feet of the rim and 75% of his attempts have come off of zero dribbles. With Mara on the floor, the offense has to adjust compared to what they can do with the rest of their center rotation. Where Isaiah Hartenstein can be a high post hub and Holmgren and Jaylin Williams can space the floor, Mara has less variability to his game. That doesn't mean he can't be effective, but it does require an adjustment on Oklahoma City's end to put him in the right spots and find ways to still create space for others when he's on the floor.

On defense, Mara gives them a needed rim protector and he's proven to be a high-caliber shot blocker already with seven blocks in five games despite relatively light minutes. However, like many young shot blockers, Mara is learning to navigate an increased minutes load without fouling. He has picked up nine fouls combined in his two games with 20-plus minutes. Defense will be Mara's calling card, and over the next two months, the Thunder will hope to see him continue learning to be impactful without fouling to maximize his time on the floor.

The Thunder never viewed this season as one to focus on development, but at this point they have little choice but to embrace that with Mara. He has the potential to be a key contributor to this team and play an extremely valuable role as they get set for a decade-long battle with the Wemby-led Spurs. With Holmgren out, he's going to get far more extended opportunities to see the floor than expected early in his rookie year, and perhaps that can pay dividends down the road for Oklahoma City.

With Williams out for the year and Wallace out for at least most of it, there were plenty of rumblings about the Thunder exploring their options on the trade market. A deal was unlikely to happen until at least December 15, when players who signed this summer become available, but Oklahoma City figured to spend the next month-plus evaluating its roster and keeping an eye on potential additions from around the league to stay in the contender realm.

With Holmgren out, one wonders whether that changes the calculus for Sam Presti -- or at least the timeline for making a move. Holmgren is expected to return in January, which would allow the Thunder to wait until he's back and see how he's performing coming off of the knee procedure for a couple of weeks before the trade deadline.

The Thunder should be able to manage two-plus months of a center rotation of Hartenstein, Williams and Mara -- with more Kenrich Williams at the four as well -- meaning their focus will still be on adding on the wing and in the backcourt.

Presti may want to see exactly what he has this season before making a significant in-season move. The Thunder could try to weather the storm with the roster they have until Holmgren returns and see where they are in the West before determining whether to make a smaller move or a more foundation-shaking trade.

No one has won three straight MVPs since Larry Bird in the 1980s. For one, it's hard to maintain that level for three straight seasons, but as we've seen over the years, even when the greats do stay in the MVP conversation, voter fatigue typically sets in after a player wins two and voters seek out someone else.

However, with the injuries piling up in Oklahoma City, if there were ever a year for a player to break that drought and become the first to three-peat as MVP in 40 years, it could be Shai Gilgeous-Alexander dragging this Thunder team to another top-four seed with such a depleted roster.

It's been a relatively slow start to the season for Gilgeous-Alexander, averaging 26.0 points, 4.6 rebounds and 3.4 assists per game on 45.9/26.5/87.5 shooting splits. That kind of production obviously won't get him a third MVP award, but if he ups his level and carries this Thunder squad without Holmgren for half the season and without Williams and Wallace for most of it, he will have to garner real consideration.

Some of his candidacy will be determined by who else is in the mix early on -- Luka Dončić seems poised to put up massive numbers in L.A. -- but the circumstances in Oklahoma City this season are so unique that Gilgeous-Alexander could break the run of back-to-back MVPs who have fallen short in pursuit of a third straight.

Gilgeous-Alexander's play will determine exactly how the Thunder proceed this season. If he plays at his typical MVP level and the Thunder look like a threat, Presti may have no choice but to try and make a splash ahead of the deadline to bring in reinforcements to chase a second championship. If it's a down year for Gilgeous-Alexander without some of his top support elements around him, perhaps there's less of a push to go all-in this season and Oklahoma City could look to ride out the storm and hope for better health in 2027-28.

The 34-17 victory in primetime was a statement. It announced to the rest of the NFL that this Bears team has entered its contention window.

No bigger opportunity exists than a road game against the defending Super Bowl champions in a standalone TV window. The entire football world watched the Bears assert control over the Seahawks in Week 8. Anyone who questioned them heading into the contest now has little reason to doubt their championship makeup.

History does offer a warning, as the last time the Bears started a season 6-2 or better through eight games, they missed the playoffs. But this year's offense is far more trustworthy than the one that collapsed in the second half of the 2012 season. Caleb Williams has leveled up to join the same conversation as the league's most elite quarterbacks, and with a potent run game by his side and a renowned play-caller in Ben Johnson orchestrating the system, Chicago's high-scoring attack has staying power.

Factor in a defense that improved noticeably with a single move ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline, and the Bears are now more than just a one-dimensional squad. Jeffery Simmons raised this squad's ceiling immensely.

The Bears own more wins by double digits than any team in the NFL. If Williams maintains his pace and Simmons continues to shine as the All-Pro defensive tackle he is, the blowouts will keep rolling in, potentially all the way to the Super Bowl.

via DraftKings Sportsbook, +1000 or better

The sports betting market already viewed Chicago as a playoff-caliber team. It held the eighth-shortest odds to win the Super Bowl heading into Week 8. That victory over the reigning champions showed how one game can change the conversation, because the Bears are now tied for the third-best title odds. Among NFC teams, only the San Francisco 49ers have a brighter outlook.

Trading two first-round picks for Simmons was an all-in move from general manager Ryan Poles. It was the kind of investment that signaled the Bears are confident in their roster's ability to contend for titles now and that adding a star defensive tackle can get them over the top. One game into his Chicago career, it appears that Poles' calculus on Simmons and his potential impact was correct. He is arguably the best interior defensive lineman in football both against the run and the pass, and he looked the part in his Bears debut.

Simmons flew relatively under the radar during his Tennessee Titans career. He was renowned in league circles but rarely played on big stages due to the Titans' perennial struggles. Now he finds himself in a major market as perhaps the best player on a prolific team. The former first-round pick's stock as a superstar is about to explode.

The Bears entered Week 8 averaging 6.3 yards per play allowed and cut that metric in half in the first game with Simmons in the lineup. Seattle managed just 3.0 yards per play and posted a 25.0% success rate when Simmons was on the field, while it produced most of its output when he was on the sideline. The numbers inflated to 13.3 yards per play and a 62.5% success rate with Simmons off the field.

"You can feel his presence out there, whether it's during the play or even after the play," Johnson said after the game. "You can feel him talking a little smack, as well, which I think that elevates everybody around him. I thought he played outstanding. He got one of the game balls. I mean, to come in there and have a share of the lead of tackles and a sack in his first game, his impact was profound."

Across 49 snaps, Simmons tied for the team lead with six tackles and five pressures. His first stop came on the game's opening play from scrimmage. He then logged his first sack as a Bear on the first play of the next series and added a second tackle for loss and a pass breakup later in the night. Despite facing more double teams (13) than any player on Chicago's defensive front, Simmons was the only Bears pass rusher to record a pressure in under two seconds, according to Next Gen Stats. That does not even take into account the stout run-stopping impact he made against a Seahawks team that was finally at full strength in its backfield.

Jeffery Simmons highlights, anyone? pic.twitter.com/AwU17TzjfC

Chicago's defense can become fundamentally different with Simmons in the equation. This is a unit that previously relied on scheming up its pass rush to affect the passer, as evidenced by its 37.6% blitz rate, the eighth-highest in the NFL. But now it does not need to send the house. Simmons can and will win at the point of attack on his own. He dominated the Seattle offensive line even with All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson joining that unit via trade ahead of the Week 8 showdown.

Simmons freeing up the rest of the defensive front could be a game-changer. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen described the trade like "waking up on Christmas morning and you go out and you see all the presents under the tree." He can now drop linebackers into coverage with more regularity and put pass rushers in positions to capitalize on the double teams Simmons will draw in the middle of the field. The impact of Simmons' arrival goes well beyond just the highlight plays he will make on his own; it could also make everyone around him better.

Johnson said before the season that he wants his offense to be the highest-scoring unit in NFL history. The Bears are well short of record pace, but they might still boast the league's most high-octane attack for the rest of the season.

Against a Seattle defense that one week ago had every possible answer for the Kansas City Chiefs and stymied the NFL's top run game, the Bears moved the ball with consistency and scored more points than any Seahawks opponent on the year. Seattle had not allowed a single point on an opponent's opening possession in 16 games before the Bears marched down the field for a 17-play touchdown drive to open the game. That was also the first time in 17 consecutive drives that the Seahawks allowed an opponent to reach the red zone.

Only one team has been able to keep the Bears in check when Williams is under center. Outside of a weather-impacted game against the Minnesota Vikings and their league-best defense, Chicago has been practically unstoppable with Williams in the lineup. It is undefeated in games that he started and finished and scored at least 30 points in each of those contests.

Running back D'Andre Swift scored three touchdowns in Seattle and is now the only player with three rushing touchdowns in multiple games this year.

Luther Burden III also continues to emerge as a standout wide receiver in his second year. He is in the midst of a breakout season and has been incredible with Williams at quarterback. Since Williams returned from his hamstring injury, Burden posted at least 56 yards in every game, scored two touchdowns and enjoyed the second-best outing of his career: A 130-yard outburst in Week 7 against the New England Patriots.

The supporting cast around Williams is chock-full of playmakers, and the MVP candidate is adept at making the most of them.

With a 6-2 record, the Bears are already significantly more accomplished than two division leaders. They will challenge the Vikings for the NFC North crown, and if they surpass Minnesota in the divisional standings, they will have a clear path to the conference's No. 1 seed come playoff time.

Chicago will be favored in its next two games at home against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and New Orleans Saints. The schedule stiffens up from there, and how the Bears perform in the gauntlet of the second half of the season will determine whether they enter the postseason as Super Bowl favorites or as challengers to the top teams in the conference. The latter outcome might be the new floor for a squad that seems fully ready to vie for the loftiest of goals.

With Williams healthy again and perhaps the best offense in football at its disposal, and with Simmons allowing the defense to do more than just hold its own, Chicago is a complete team capable of standing atop the NFL at season's end.

#2625. Astros hire Randy Flores as new general manager as offseason filled with questions begins in Houston

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros' search for a new head of baseball operations has ended with the hiring of Randy Flores as general manager. The 51-year-old Flores had been an assistant general manager with the St. Louis Cardinals. In Houston, Flores replaces Dana Brown, who was let go in late August. Flores becomes the fourth head of baseball operations to serve under Astros owner Jim Crane.

"Randy has had a huge impact on the Cardinals over the last 10 seasons," Crane said in a statement released by the club. "Throughout the entire interview process, we've been thoroughly impressed with Randy and his background in scouting and player acquisition. We're happy to welcome Randy and his family to the Astros and we can't wait to get to work on bringing another championship to Houston."

Added Flores: "I am excited and grateful for this amazing opportunity. The Astros have a long winning tradition under Jim Crane, and I look forward to contributing to the success.  I want to thank the Cardinals organization for the opportunities and support that made this next chapter possible. My family and I are excited to make Houston home."

Flores for roughly a decade served as scouting director for the Cardinals and was tasked with running their draft. He added the assistant GM title in 2018 and saw his portfolio of responsibilities expand within the last year.

Flores takes over an Astros organization beset by uncertainty. With an aging roster and after several key departures over the years, the Astros have seen their season-long win total decline for four straight years. This past season, the Astros eked out the American League Central title but finished with a .500 record and a negative run differential. In terms of success and roster strength, they're a long way from their dynasty years of 2017-22. It's not certain whether the Astros moving forward will try to squeeze out another season of relevance or embrace a rebuild, but either path will have its challenges.

Speaking of challenges, Crane and his trusted advisor Jeff Bagwell have been an increasingly meddlesome presence in recent years, and it's unclear to what degree Flores will have autonomy in his role. Whatever the future holds, Flores' first major decision is filling the managerial vacancy. After the end of the regular season, Crane opted not to renew the contract of former manager Joe Espada.

Prior to beginning his front office career, Flores spent parts of eight seasons in the majors as a left-handed reliever. In 2006, he earned a World Series ring as a member of that Cardinals team.

#2623. Luka Dončić teaches Yaxel Lendeborg a lesson, but Warriors bail their rookie out in comeback win over Lakers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When Yaxel Lendeborg decided it would be a good idea to start a war of words with Luka Dončić during and after his first career NBA game, basically calling the Lakers superstar a flopping crybaby for whom he "lost all respect," both Stephen Curry and Steve Kerr had the same message for their brash rookie.

Friday night was Lendeborg's chance to do just that when the Warriors hosted Dončić and the Lakers for the start of the NBA Cup's group stage. It did not, to put it politely, go well for Lendeborg, who laid down the worst track of his young career with six points, one rebound, zero assists and five turnovers.

Lendeborg got into early foul trouble and was never a factor on either end. For a guy who has injected so much juice into what looked like an old, disinterested, almost lifeless Warriors team when it faced these same Lakers on opening night, Lendeborg was all but invisible in finishing as a game-low minus-20 in his 24 minutes before fouling out.

When asked what lesson he had taken from a performance like this after shining such a spotlight on himself with the Luka comments, and what he might do differently next time, Lendeborg, with the same brutal honest he has shown at every turn, said he would "try not to wet the bed as bad as I did."

Meanwhile, Dončić -- who was egging on the "Luka sucks!" chant coming from the Chase Center crowd early on -- poured in 21 first-quarter points en route to 37 for the game. He added seven rebounds, five assists, a pair of blocks and a steal for good measure. He outscored the entire Warriors team in the first quarter by himself as the Lakers raced out to a 25-point first-half lead.

Luka Doncic’s face after hitting a 3 over Yaxel Lendeborg 😂 pic.twitter.com/CAiF7LUxDz

Certainly everything you've read so far would suggest the Lakers ran away with this game, but in today's NBA, a 20-point lead is just prologue for a second-half plot twist. And sure enough, the Warriors, behind eight 3-pointers and 31 points from Curry, stormed back to win going away, 112-95, for their third straight victory after opening the season 0-3.

Lendeborg might not have been able to back up his Dončić talk (which, we have to point out, was nothing but the truth, even if you could argue he would've been better off keeping it to himself, at least this early in his career), but the greatest shooter to ever set foot on this planet had his back. This is how you go at Luka Dončić ...

A 3PT MASTERCLASS FROM STEPHEN 📺 @NBAonPrime pic.twitter.com/nIIyrtmuKM

STOP IT, STEPH 🥵 pic.twitter.com/8ns53YenN2

It wasn't just Curry -- who passed Dominique Wilkins for 18th on the NBA's all-time scoring list -- coming to Lendeborg's rescue. It was Brandin Podziemski with 21 points, six assists and five rebounds. It was De'Anthony Melton and Georges Niang tag-teaming for 27 points and seven 3-pointers. It was Draymond Green taking over the Dončić defensive duties and dishing out nine dimes. It was the Warriors' bench outscoring L.A.'s bench 50-7, and a defense that held the Lakers to just 57 points over the final three quarters to fuel an astounding 42-point turnaround.

For Lendeborg, there's a lesson here that goes beyond not riling up a superstar and letting your play do the talking (which, I will restate, was fine; he's a grown man, and he didn't say anything that everyone else doesn't think), which is that it ultimately doesn't matter that Dončić got the better of him individually on Friday, because in the end it was the Warriors that got the better of the Lakers.

This was the message that Kerr had for Lendeborg after the opener in which Lendeborg was all too proud of his individual defense on Dončić.

"He did a good job on Luka one-on-one, but we got torched by Luka as a team," Kerr said. "All those stats that the NBA puts up, like, 'Hey, when he guarded him, who the eff cares?' It's like, they scored 127 on us. That stuff's all bulls---. It's our defense."

Translation: it's a team game. As his career progresses, Lendeborg, a clear alpha, is going to be the one picking up his teammates on plenty of nights, but on this night it was the rookie who needed his teammates to cover for him. Suffice it to say, they did that, and Lendeborg, to his credit, recognized the effort with genuine humility.

"Them boys had my back today," Lendeborg said, noting that in his effort to stay calm and not let the hype of the matchup take over, he actually stayed "a little too calm" and never got into a groove. "Steph Curry, again, did his thing. The bench mob showed up today. It was awesome. They all played a great game. I feel like I was the only Debbie downer on the team. I feel like next time I get into one of these games, just try to be that guy sucking up all the energy."

#2622. Klint Kubiak addresses Ashton Jeanty's disappearance from game plan vs. Jets

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Last Sunday against the New York Jets, Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty — the No. 6 overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft — saw his workload cut to season lows pretty much across the board.

Jeanty carried the ball just twice, gaining only 9 yards on the ground. He also played only 39.7% of the team's offensive snaps, a new low this season by over 13 percentage points. Nominal backup Mike Washington Jr., a fourth-round rookie, saw a season-high 25 carries and a 60.3% snap share that was his highest by over 25 percentage points.

Raiders coach Klint Kubiak explained the reversal of fortunes during his Monday media session with reporters.

"I stand by what I said (Sunday) that we're going to need Mike, we're going to need Ashton, we're going to need Dylan (Laube)," Kubiaksaid. "They're all part of our success, run and pass. Ashton made huge plays for us in the pass game. He was phenomenal in protection like he's always been. The way the game went yesterday, Mike got more carries. Going forward, we're going to be counting on all three of those guys."

Jeanty did make a few nice plays in the passing game, catching three of four passes thrown his way and racking up 64 yards through the air. He has been an effective pass catcher this season, hauling in 37 of 48 targets for 376 yards and three touchdowns. His work in that area stands in stark contrast to his ineffectiveness on the ground, where he is averaging just 3.1 yards per carry and looking not one bit like the explosive playmaker he was at Boise State.

It's likely that inefficiency is pushing the Raiders to funnel more work to Washington, who is averaging 4.3 yards per carry. That's not tremendously efficient, either, but it's a lot better than 3.1 per carry. Still, Kubiak noted that the distribution of touches and snaps might not be the same every week.

"I think it's always a moving target. You see where your team is at and who's playing the best ball at the time. It's a 17-game regular season where things change every week," Kubiak said. "That's the NFL. We have a young roster and we're going to give guys opportunities and see what fits us best. But your 11, whether you're playing really well or not playing well at all, it's always going to change a little bit."

It's also worth noting that Jeanty's workload reduction came after he called out the Jets' defense in the lead-up to the game.

"I think we can definitely get the run game going, get back on track and just really get after these guys," Jeanty said last week, via the New York Post. "Couple of guys out there that don't really want to tackle, but I'm not going to say names."

The Raiders ended up winning the game, but not on the strength of their rushing attack, which yielded just 2.9 yards per carry on 33 attempts. It was Kirk Cousins and the passing offense that carried Las Vegas to a win.

After snapping their four-game losing streak with a win over New York, the Raiders have a tough upcoming schedule. They travel to San Francisco to take on the 49ers this weekend, then host the Seattle Seahawks before visiting the Denver Broncos. It'll be tough to get the ground game going against those opponents, too, but it'll still be interesting to watch how the backfield split shakes itself out during that time, and whether Jeanty falls even further out of favor.

#2621. MLB rumors: Padres decline option on key rotation piece, Korean star to be posted

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only four days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Sunday's hot stove happenings.

San Diego's top two starters are now free agents. Two days after Michael King exercised an opt-out clause to become a free agent, the Padres declined their $14 million club option on Nick Pivetta, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Had the Padres picked up the option, Pivetta would have held an $18 million player option for 2028. That surely factored into the team's decision.

Pivetta, 34 in February, missed roughly five months with a flexor strain this past season. He returned late in the season and pitched reasonably well in six starts spanning September and the postseason. The San Diego Union-Tribune notes the Padres still have concerns about Pivetta's elbow, but could re-sign him to a new contract with a lower salary and/or no player option.

San Diego signed Pivetta to what amounted to a two-year, $23 million contact with two players options in February 2025. The flexor strain triggered an injury clause that converted the 2027 player option into a club option. We ranked Pivetta as the offseason's 43rd-best free agent.

As expected, the Orioles have declined their $20 million club option for center fielder Luis Robert Jr., reports ESPN. They will pay him a $2 million buyout, so it was functionally an $18 million decision. Robert suffered a hamstring injury and played only three games with the O's after being claimed off waivers from the Mets in late September.

Now 29, Robert again had multiple stints on the injured list this past season. He continued to punish lefties and play solid center field defense when healthy, but injuries have limited him to only 271 of 489 possible regular-season games from 2024-26. We did not rank Robert among our top 50 free agents, though he is an interesting upside play given his age.

The Hanwha Eagles of the Korea Baseball Organization will post star third baseman Si-Hwan Roh for MLB teams this offseason, reports Yonhap News Agency. Roh signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and $23 million), though as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the team once his MLB stint is over.

Roh, 26, has been one of the KBO's best players the last several years. He hit .283/.360/.505 with 29 home runs in 2026, and has averaged 35 home runs per 162 games since 2023. Roh is considered a reliable but unspectacular defender at third, plus he has first base experience as well. This free agent class is very thin at the hot corner. Roh should generate a good deal of interest.

KBO players get a 30-day negotiating window once officially posted. If Roh does not sign with an MLB team during the 30-day window, he will return to the Eagles. It's possible that Roh, a right-handed hitter, will eclipse his $23 million guarantee with the Eagles over just a handful of years with an MLB team.

The Astros have acquired Triple-A righty reliever Evan Reifert from the Rays for cash, reports the Tampa Bay Times. Houston is likely to add him to their 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. The Rays did not have the roster space to do that, so they traded for cash rather than lose him for nothing. Reifert, 27, has an excellent slider and used it to strike out 81 batters in 58 Triple-A innings in 2026. He should spend time in Houston's bullpen next season.

#2619. Could NFC North have four playoff teams? After strong Week 8, it's looking more likely than ever

The NFC North had a good Week 8. Very good. The Packers kicked the week off by beating the Panthers, and the Bears ended the week by throttling the reigning-champion Seahawks. In between, the Lions beat the previously unbeaten Vikings, making a historically competitive division even more competitive.

Through eight weeks, the NFC North as a collective is 22-8. That's not only by far the best in the NFL this season, but the third-best mark by any division through eight weeks since the 1970 AFL-NFL merger. Only the 2022 NFC East has been better.

All that leads us to this: The NFC North is staring down the distinct possibility of becoming the first division to produce four playoff teams since the 2002 realignment to four divisions within each conference. In fact, if the playoffs started today, the NFC North would have four playoff teams in the playoffs.

Here's what the latest SportsLine projections say about the possibility.

If we multiply the odds above together, the NFC North's chance to have all four teams in the postseason sits at about 36% -- which is still really, really, historically good. It just shows how hard it is.

The NFC North will need more weeks like Week 8, when the two teams playing outside the division shone while the playoff-hopeful teams outside the division didn't. Think more results like the Cowboys blowing it against the Cardinals and the Seahawks losing to the Bears.

When the NFL only had three divisions per conference (1970-2001), three divisions produced four playoff teams in a single season.

So, none of those divisions produced a Super Bowl winner, and only one produced a conference champion. Thirty-ish years later, though, that really shouldn't inform how we view the NFC North teams' chances to win it all. It was a whole different world back then.

Under the current division alignment, having four playoff teams has been possible only since 2020, when the playoffs expanded to seven teams per conference. Since then, seven divisions have produced three playoff teams in a season. But all of those teams had a notable weak link. The excellent NFC North last year had the 3-14 Cardinals. The excellent 2024 NFC North had the 5-12 Bears. the list goes on.

The 2023 AFC North came the closest, with all four teams having winning records but the 9-8 Bengals finishing as the eighth seed in the conference, just barely missing out. The Packers are a historically strong "weak link" as we've already discussed, but it wouldn't be unreasonable to see a scenario in which they -- or another NFC North team -- just miss out.

There's a long way to go. Can the Packers continue to overcome their historic run woes? Green Bay is averaging 60.6 rushing yards per game, on pace to be the worst since the merger. Can Jordan Love and the passing game continue to carry such a heavy load, especially when the weather turns? Can the Vikings continue winning with one of the worst offenses in the NFL? Are the Lions' recent defensive improvements real? Can the Bears live with shaky secondary play? These teams are all quite good; none are perfect.

Still, there's not a ton in the way. The NFC East and NFC South look like one-bid divisions, with the Eagles going through a worst-case scenario year and the Cowboys not far behind. The NFC West has also been quite disappointing. Both the preseason Super Bowl favorites (the Rams) and the reigning champs (the Seahawks) are just 4-4.

Seattle is the real thing standing in the way currently. SportsLine gives the Seahawks a 58% chance to go to the postseason, just ahead of the Packers. The Seahawks do get an easier stretch upcoming to get back on track; NFC North teams will be hoping they stumble against teams such as the Cardinals, Raiders, Cowboys and/or Giants, four of their next five opponents. And of course, it'd be unwise to count out the Rams, who are getting Myles Garrett back to practice this week.

It's clear the NFC North is the dominant division in the NFL in terms of both top-tier contenders and depth. Thirty-five percent doesn't sound great, but the conference as a whole is startlingly thin. Right now, I'd lean toward the NFC North getting all four teams in, but it's a very slight lean. How the Seahawks and the Rams handle the next few weeks will be crucial.

#2618. Mets legend Jerry Koosman dies at 83: Pitcher helped New York win 1969 World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Mets team Hall of Famer and two-time All-Star Jerry Koosman died Sunday morning in Osceola, Wisconsin, the team announced. He was 83. The Mets say Koosman battled multiple illnesses before his death.

"Kooz was one of the greatest pitchers in team history and a beloved member of the Mets family," Mets owners Alex and Steve Cohen said in a statement. "The 1969 Miracle Mets were filled with heroes, and the special southpaw from Appleton, Minnesota, was central to their success. He was a fierce competitor on the field, and respected teammate in the clubhouse. His legendary performance in the World Series helped the Mets secure their first Championship in team history. On behalf of the entire Mets organization, we extend our heartfelt condolences to Jerry's family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him."

The Mets discovered Koosman while he was pitching for the United States Army and signed him to a contract in August 1964. He made his MLB debut in April 1967 and moved into the rotation full-time the next season. Koosman threw 263 ⅔ innings with a 2.08 ERA as a rookie in 1968, which earned him an All-Star Game selection and MVP votes, and a second-place finish in the Rookie of the Year voting behind Hall of Famer Johnny Bench.

In 1969, Koosman was again an All-Star, throwing 241 innings with a 2.28 ERA. He was New York's No. 2 starter in the postseason between Hall of Famers Tom Seaver and Nolan Ryan. Koosman made two starts for the Miracle Mets in the World Series, including the Game 5 clincher against the Baltimore Orioles. He allowed three runs in the complete game win and recorded all but one possible out in his two World Series starts.

From 1968-76, Koosman was simply one of the best pitchers in the game, pitching to a 2.94 ERA and averaging 223 innings per season. The Mets traded him to the Minnesota Twins for Jesse Orosco in December 1978 and Koosman finished his career with stints for the Twins (1979-81), Chicago White Sox (1981-83), and Philadelphia Phillies (1984-85).

Koosman retired following the 1985 season with a 222-209 record and a 3.36 ERA that is 39th among AL/NL pitchers with at least 3,500 career innings. He ranks 35th all-time in strikeouts (2,556), 40th all-time in starts (527), 48th all-time in innings (3,839 ⅓), and 77th all-time in pitching WAR (57.0). Koosman went to two All-Star Games and finished second to Randy Jones in the 1976 Cy Young voting.

The Mets inducted Koosman into their Hall of Fame in 1989 and retired his No. 36 in 2021. His 140 wins are the most in franchise history among left-handers and third in team history overall, behind Seaver (198) and Dwight Gooden (157). Koosman is second in Mets history in innings (behind Seaver) and third in strikeouts (behind Seaver and Gooden).

Koosman fell off the Baseball Writers Association of America's Hall of Fame ballot in 1991, his first year of eligibility.

#2617. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2616. Beware of the Lion – TSV 1860 Munich can still mix with the Bundesliga's best

MÜNCHEN (Bulinews): On our excursion to München last weekend, naturally topping the list of priorities was the Bundesliga's famed Der Klassiker as FC Bayern Munich hosted Borussia Dortmund on Saturday, 31 October. One could be forgiven for having tunnel vision.

To that, I would say do that at your own peril. The Friday prior to the bright lights of the Allianz Arena also served up a footballing delight in the vibrant southeastern suburb of Giesing. The might of TSV 1860 Munich taking on Regionalliga Bavaria rivals TSV Buchbach.

Four tier of German football you say? Fear not. A whopping 15,000 fans – of which maybe 1000 are Buchbach supporters – filter into the Grünwalder Stadion. The noise is already reaching fever pitch as we wind our way up the concrete steps of the South Stand.

Shortly after, the whistle blows to get the ball rolling. The football is nothing short of brilliant either. That blend of gritty 50-50 duels with no shirking out, coupled with some technical excellence. Namely, Buchbach's No.10 Tobias Heiland who neatly curled in the opening goal.

𝘋𝘪𝘦 𝘓ö𝘸𝘦𝘯 (The Lions) hit back in a flash. Ex-FC Augsburg star Florian Niederlechner and Felix Weber find the net. Still, Buchbach find a response. Heiland again with a sweet half-volley on the edge of the box before Samed Bahar's drive finds the bottom corner.

In need of a refreshment after a half that ended 3-2 to the guests, we make our way to the kiosk. As if the night couldn't get any more interesting, my colleague Manuel Veth of The Gegenpressing Podcast and I happen to bump into the referee's father there.

Overhearing some 1860 fans mulling over his son's first-half calls, he smiles but you sense a hint of paternal worry. The arbiter in question is 26-year-old Johannes Wagner – it was his first time officiating at this level. Might I add, he went on to do an exemplary job of it too.

Into the catacombs we go for an interval meeting with 1860 president Gernot Mang. There's no fancy murals or glitzy design to the interior. You must duck under the stand's support beams to avoid hitting your head. But that's football. Real football. I find it charming.

Mang is a charismatic, calmly spoken but passionate man who confesses his and the club's aim of returning to the Bundesliga – something they've missed since 2004. This isn't some crazed pipe dream. It's a mission. It may take time, but Giesing wasn't built in a day.

Back to our press box for the second helping of what seemed destined to be inevitable chaos. That's exactly what happens. Both sides had chances but Arian Calderon heads in from six yards for the hosts. We're tired at 3-3 with 8 minutes to play plus injury time.

With the clock hitting 90+4 minutes, space was afforded to Lance Fiedler. Buchbach stood off enabling the left-back to hammer a shot inside the left upright. Cue pandemonium in the terraces. You can't help but get caught up in it. Even the steward beside us delights.

Chants of "𝘌𝘪𝘯𝘮𝘢𝘭 𝘓ö𝘸𝘦, 𝘐𝘮𝘮𝘦𝘳 𝘓ö𝘸𝘦" (Once a Lion, forever a Lion) fill the cool Munich air. The three points sees them rise to second in the table. After the emotional rollercoaster, the party continues in Bamboleo – a 𝘒𝘯𝘦𝘪𝘱𝘦 – your unpretentious, cozy local matchday bar.

Sure, the allure of FC Bayern and BVB may have dominated the weekend. But in a way, the 1860 atmosphere is unfiltered and unmatched. One could argue it even surpasses their arch rivals in red and merits a hasty return to Germany's topflight.

Things may not be entirely harmonious behind the scenes after majority shareholder Hasan Ismaik's exit. However, the football drops jaws and the fans remain unwavering. A lion is the king of the jungle. It's fearless, resilient and untamable – TSV 1860 Munich embodies it all.

#2614. Jeanie Buss accuses siblings of conspiring against her as dispute over Lakers stake continues

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Jeanie Buss has accused her siblings of conspiring against her in a "cloak and dagger" campaign through the media in a court filing this week and has asked a judge to block her siblings' attempts to sell the family's shares of the Los Angeles Lakers, ESPN reports.

According to Wednesday's filing, Jeanie Buss said her siblings -- specifically Joey and Jesse Buss -- are jealous of their father's decision to leave her with governor rights to the team and she does not want them selling the family's remaining shares of the team.

Finality for both sides of the legal spat could come during a scheduled Dec. 8 hearing in Los Angeles Superior Court.

Former Disney CEO Bob Iger and Josh Kushner spearhead an ownership group looking to buy the Lakers from Mark Walter at a valuation of $12.5 billion.

"The conflicts that ensued after Dr. (Jerry) Buss's death (in 2013) were sadly inevitable, and no doubt intensified given that Dr. Buss chose his daughter over four sons to be his successor," representation for Jeanie Buss wrote in this week's filing. "Respondents' obsession with tearing down Jeanie and their inability to accept that she would be a part of the Lakers' future is borne of this classic succession parable."

Jeanie Buss would no longer serve as the Lakers' governor if her family sells its 17.8% ownership stake, which is just above the NBA's 15% minimum for the family to retain control. Iger previously said during an interview with The California Post that the plan was for Buss to remain governor, but "if things change, they'll change."

The latest filing continues an ongoing saga between family members over the NBA's third-most valuable franchise. Earlier this year, ESPN reported that Jeanie Buss contended that a 2017 court order prevents any vote to sell the remaining family shares without her consent.

That was not the first time that the Buss siblings have fought over control of the team. When Jeanie fired Jim Buss as head of basketball operations in 2017, he and Johnny Buss attempted to strip Jeanie of her seat on the Lakers' board of directors.

The two sides ultimately agreed to settle with Jeanie Buss remaining in control of the team.

Now, Jeanie Buss is asking the court to remove two siblings as co-trustees of the trust for breach of fiduciary duty, hold them in contempt of court, and "find Jim, Johnny and Jesse liable for aiding and abetting a violation of the 2017 court order and be reimbursed for legal costs," per ESPN.

If the Buss family sells the entirety of its shares of the team, each sibling receives an additional $371 million per go-along rights. ESPN reported this week that settlement talks have begun.

"Jeanie had no choice but to seek court intervention to enforce the clear terms of the trust and this court's 2017 order," Wednesday's filing states. "Respondents respond (by) casting themselves as victims, when in reality, the entire episode is their own false flag operation.

"The cloak and dagger, backroom 'votes' and 'resolutions' shared with ESPN, rather than their co-trustee and sister, and subsequent refusal to discuss the matter, was intended to force Jeanie's hand, cry victim and again smear her in the media by sharing in advance their specious response."
